author: sorrel
body:
Stacked on #33 — review that first, or read this diff alone, which is only this work.

## The finding

Auto mode was already safe against doing the wrong thing: files only, never bins, never touches mail a guard held back, every move journalled and undoable. What it could not protect against was the *right* thing done to mail that wanted eyes on it — filed correctly, quietly, at half past eight.

Measured against `guards.needs_attention`, with a `List-Unsubscribe` header supplied so each message had every chance of being held:

| Sender | Subject | Guard |
|---|---|---|
| `notifications@code-host.example` | Dependabot alert: critical vulnerability | **files** |
| `no-reply@accounts.search-co.example` | Security alert: new sign-in | **files** |
| `no-reply@signin.cloud-co.example` | Root account was accessed | **files** |
| `noreply@breach-check.example` | You have been pwned in a breach | **files** |

Not one held. Structural, not a bug: `_NO_REPLY_WORDS` contains `"notifications"` and `"noreply"`, so `is_bulk` settles them from the address alone and `needs_attention` returns before a header is read. Correct for the question that guard asks — nobody awaits a reply to a Dependabot alert — but not the only question. And these are the senders auto mode is *surest* about: high volume, consistent, long filing history. A breach notice reads 0.97 and files itself.

## The guard

`security.py` holds such mail in the inbox, whatever the confidence and whatever rule names the sender. Applied outermost, so it wins the label when a message trips more than one; the only guard that carries `held_folder` through, since filing security mail where it would have gone is what most of it wants once read. Never binnable; always offered in `review_held`, which is the attended case its claim excludes.

**Worth arguing with:** this guard is deliberately *broader* than the others. The asymmetry runs opposite to the reply guard's — there a false negative loses a message wanting an answer, so it is narrow; here both directions fail into the inbox, so a false positive costs one message filed by hand. The limit on that generosity is usefulness, not safety, which is a question about this mailbox rather than the word list. So it was measured:

```
178 of 13,993 filed messages (1.3%) would be held back.
40 security alert / 22 new sign-in / 12 verification code / 11 password reset
/ 10 new login / 9 new device / 8 two-factor / ... 30 distinct terms,
tailing off into individual CVEs.
```

No term running away with it, a long specific tail, comfortably under the 10% at which the vocabulary would have been cut. It stands as written.

## Also

- **`mail-triage report`** — the regular part. Leads with what the guard held, in full and by subject; counts everything else.
- **`auto_limit`** (default 50) bounds one unattended run and keeps it undoable as a single journal run. Most confident first; the rest wait.
- **`contrib/com.mail-triage.auto.plist`** — a LaunchAgent template, deliberately **not installed**. A schedule that moves real mail unattended for ever is the largest version of the second safety rule; fill in two paths and `launchctl load` it yourself.
- `mail-triage security --add/--forget/--measure`.

Spec at `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-17-auto-mode-security.md`.

1038 tests pass. `FakeMail` and the suite only; `--measure` is read-only.

body:
The last milestone. Based on `feature/m9-images` rather than `main`, since #10 is not merged yet — merge that one first and this rebases onto it.

## The hole in the first rule

`docs/DESIGN.md` forbids a blank canvas, and that was only enforced at the door: an empty document is never restored. Mid-session nothing enforced it, and select-all-delete is two keystrokes from a blank editor beside a blank sheet with nothing on screen to ask for anything.

The empty document now says what it is and offers the way back, and the toolbar carries the **New** the offer needed anyway. New asks before it acts, and only when there is something to lose — an untouched document is replaced in silence, because a confirmation in front of nothing is a habit rather than a question.

## The app on a phone

Two 50/50 resizable panes at 390px is 195px of editor beside 195px of A4. Below `md` the split gives way to a Source / Document switch, and the settings panel takes the pane instead of sitting beside it.

The rule that makes it work is that **neither pane is ever unmounted, only hidden** — otherwise printing from the Source tab would print nothing. Verified by printing from a 390px viewport with the source in front: 3 pages, 215.9 × 279.4 mm, 22 mm margins, diagram drawn — the same file as from 1440px.

A second, wider threshold decides only a default: below 1024 the panel starts closed, because two panes *and* a 288px panel left the document 240px.

## Accessibility

Four defects, each with an address:

- **The editor was a keyboard trap.** Tab indents, which is what Markdown editors do, so **Escape** now opens a two-second window in which Tab moves focus — CodeMirror's own tab-focus mode, bound to the key people try rather than the Ctrl-m nobody guesses. Chained, not overridden.
- **Nothing was named.** The one text box was announced as "edit text"; the document pane, the settings panel and the resize separator had no names at all. The accessibility tree now reads back a name for every landmark and control.
- **The focus ring failed 1.4.11** at 2.3:1 against white. Darkened to 4.4:1.
- **Nothing answered `prefers-reduced-motion`.**

Plus a skip link past the editor.

## Launch materials

- **Screenshots by script.** `scripts/screenshot.mjs` drives the same real Chrome `print-to-pdf.mjs` does and produces the three README images plus the social card, so they can be made again the day the design moves.
- **The README's privacy paragraph was wrong** — it still claimed fonts and themes come from a CDN, which stopped being true at M3. Of all the paragraphs to be wrong about.
- `CONTRIBUTING.md`, mostly about scope: five controls on purpose, the two rules that cannot bend.
- `og:`/`twitter:` meta and a `<noscript>`.
- `lane-todo.png` deleted — 51KB of screenshot committed by accident at the root of a public repo.

## What the cross-browser pass found

Firefox and WebKit, which M9 had left untested. Firefox needed nothing. WebKit has no WebP encoder in the build tested, which finally ran the fallback M9 wrote and never executed — and found it deciding badly: it asked whether the *source file* was a JPEG, where the real question is whether the pixels are opaque. A pasted screenshot was being stored at **1804KB instead of 79KB**. It now reads the alpha channel of the canvas it already drew, with the threshold at 250 rather than 255 because WebKit's gradient dithering leaves a sixth of the pixels one short of opaque. An image with a genuine hole in it still comes back as PNG; Chrome never reaches any of this.

## Verified

`test` · `lint` · `check-types` · `build` · `format:check`, and in real browsers: printing from the narrow layout and from the wide one, an empty document printing as a blank page rather than one with an invitation on it, the sample document still 10 pages at A4/22mm, the keyboard from the address bar through every stop and out of the editor, the accessibility tree, the layout at 390/767/768/900/1023/1024/1440, and image paste and HTML export in Chrome, Firefox and WebKit.

**Not verified:** VoiceOver itself — the accessibility tree was read out of the browser, which is the machine-readable half of that check. And Safari proper: the WebKit here is Playwright's build, which is the same engine family but not the shipping browser. Printing could not be driven in Firefox or WebKit at all.

author: birdayz
body:
Follow-on to #752. That PR closed RFC-232 but left the planner slower than
master; this one attacks the gap and pins the hazard the fix introduced.

## The regression, and what it actually was

The RFC-232 slowdown is **diffuse**. Profiling against a 4.1ms/op gap found no
node above ~2% — there is no hot spot to delete, because exact-type resolution
made every `FieldValue` do slightly more work everywhere. The one structural
win available is that the memo pays for a plan's structural key far more often
than it needs to.

`HashCodeWithoutChildren` rebuilt a whole `structuralKey` on every call, and
the memo's insert path calls it once per MEMBER per insert — `memoizeLeaf`
compares `member.HashCodeWithoutChildren() == h` for every member of every leaf
`Reference` before it may try equality. So the hash was paid once per plan *per
comparison*, inside a nested loop. Java pays it once per object
(`Suppliers.memoize(this::computeHashCodeWithoutChildren)` on
`AbstractRelationalExpression`); this is that memo.

Measured on `TestStatsInvariant_PurePlannerSweep`, against the true merge-base:

| | wall clock | vs master |
|---|---|---|
| master | 149.50s | 1.000x |
| RFC-232, pre-memo | 176.97s | 1.184x |
| RFC-232, memoized | 171.95s | **1.150x** |

The 1M end-to-end suite is 1.020x, i.e. the residue is planner-bound and small
relative to execution.

Instrumenting the cell over that same sweep: 3,071,048 reads against 649,360
distinct owners — ~4.7 hash requests per object, which is exactly the
repetition the memo exists to collapse.

```
reads=3071048  HIT=2223470 (72.4%)  MISS_EMPTY=649360 (21.1%)  MISS_FOREIGN=198218 (6.5%)
               storeOK=649360        storeDeclined=198218
```

`storeOK` equals `MISS_EMPTY` exactly and `storeDeclined` equals `MISS_FOREIGN`
exactly: every empty miss stores, every foreign miss declines, nothing else
happens, over three million operations.

That census also **prices the remaining lever and rejects it**. Converting the
6.5% foreign misses to hits would move `0.065 x 3.9% ~= 0.25%` of planner time,
in exchange for loosening the field whose immutability is the entire reason no
atomic sits on the plan struct, across ~57 copy sites. Rejected by measurement
rather than by taste; the number is recorded so nobody re-derives it.

## Why the memo lives behind a pointer

A plan is copied by value everywhere: `cp := *p; cp.field = x; return &cp` is
the prescribed rebuild form, enforced by `copy_method_rebuild`. That rules out
an atomic on the plan (every atomic carries `noCopy`, so `go vet`'s copylocks
would reject all ~57 copies) and equally rules out a plain two-word memo (a
shallow copy would inherit it and read another plan's hash as its own).

An atomic reached *through* a pointer is never itself copied. The plan holds a
`*hashMemoCell`; copying the plan copies the pointer. The owner check is
enforced on BOTH sides — a copy that finds the cell foreign-owned computes and
declines to store, because an unconditional store would make the two evict each
other on every comparison.

The cell starts empty, and laziness is a **correctness requirement, not an
optimisation**: several plans finish initialising after their constructor
returns (the `WithQuantifiers` paths write `drivingAlias`,
`outputNameOverrides`, `distinctProofIndexName`, all of which are in the key),
so a hash taken in the constructor would describe a plan that does not exist yet.

## The hazard the memo created

`SetInValues`, `SetSourceKind` and `SetInSources` assigned to their receivers.
`inValues` and `inSources` are in their plans' `structuralKey`.

Before the memo this was latent — the key was re-derived per comparison, so a
mutated plan simply compared as its new self. The memo makes it live and
silent: an in-place write leaves the pointer identical, so the owner check
passes and serves the **pre-mutation hash for post-mutation content**. Two
different plans intern as one and whichever was filed first wins. The check
compares identity, not content, so no refinement of it could ever catch this.

Nothing was ever wrong, because all five call sites happened to construct, set,
then yield — an ordering stated nowhere and tested by nothing. All three now
return copies.

The pin is a ratchet over the **67 types whose fields ARE memo identity** (those
defining `structuralKey`, `HashCodeWithoutChildren` or `EqualsWithoutChildren`).
Membership is derived from the tree, not listed. Zero findings, no allowlist.
It is the sibling of `copy_method_rebuild`, and the division is exact: that gate
polices HOW a copy is built; this one polices THAT a copy is built at all.

The detector's first draft did not descend through `ast.SelectorExpr`, so
`p.field = v` — the plain shape, and the form all three setters had — matched
nothing. Injecting a real receiver write into a real plan file made the census
still print `0`. That is a gate reporting green over a live defect, which is
worse than no gate; the plain-selector arm is pinned first for that reason.
Nine recall arms and seven precision arms, plus a population floor watched for
COLLAPSE rather than growth.

## Verification

- Full suite green (89/89) at the pre-rebase head; rebase onto master verified
  content-neutral (empty `git diff` against the pre-rebase tree).
- `-race` green on `plans` and `cascades`.
- Memo rollout verified mechanically: 84 `cachedStructuralHash(p)` /
  `storeStructuralHash(p, ...)` sites — 42 types x 2 — and zero sites passing an
  owner other than `p`.
- Every correction is mutation-pinned, and the pins redden **disjoint** arms:
  dropping the read-side owner check fails only the inheritance test; dropping
  the write-side check fails only the eviction test; injecting a receiver write
  fails only the ratchet, naming file:line:method; renaming the contract methods
  fails only the population floor.

## Gate status

- **Graefe**: ACK on the RFC and on the implementation, with the memo mechanism
  independently mutation-verified and the census run on the right population.
- **Torvalds**: ACK on the memo delta with one finding — *the memo turns
  in-place builders from latent into live, and nothing gates that shape*. That
  finding is what the last two commits are.
- **@claude**: ACK.
- **codex**: quota-blocked until Aug 20 (verified by probe), not skipped.

The final two commits (the setter conversion and the gate) postdate the Graefe
and @claude ACKs, so they need a delta re-confirmation before merge — an ACK
covers only the head it reviewed.

author: n-gibs
body:
worker-02 booted with three kernel parameters set by hand in `/etc/default/grub`:

```
nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off
```

Nothing in this repo recorded them. Three nodes that read as identical in git were booting with different power management, and the reason was unrecoverable. This puts the exception in `host_vars` and drops the two parameters that were never doing anything.

## Why the flags existed

The WD PC SN740 in worker-02 stopped answering shortly after boot. That is a real fault and the workaround stays, in a narrower form.

Only `nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us` was doing that job. `pcie_aspm=off` tells Linux not to *manage* ASPM; it does not disable it. The BIOS enabled ASPM on that link and Linux left it alone:

```
kernel: PCIe ASPM is disabled
lspci:  LnkCtl: ASPM L1 Enabled
        L1SubCtl1: PCI-PM_L1.2+ ASPM_L1.2+
```

The drive has run 16 days with ASPM L1.2 active, so that parameter was not what kept it attached. It also costs the kernel PCIe `_OSC` control (`acpi PNP0A08:00: _OSC: not requesting OS control`). Both PCIe parameters are dropped.

## Why 5000

`nvme-cli` is added to the base packages because `smartctl` cannot read the power-state table. The SN740 reports:

| State | Power | Exit latency | Under the new cap |
|-------|-------|--------------|-------------------|
| ps3 | 0.0150 W | 2500 µs | allowed |
| ps4 | 0.0050 W | 6000 µs | blocked |
| ps5 | 0.0033 W | 25000 µs | blocked |

The kernel filters candidate states on exit latency, so `5000` keeps ps3 and blocks the two below it.

The states being given up are worth 0.010 W. ps3 already takes the drive from ps0's 0.30 W idle down to 0.0150 W, which is all but a rounding error of the available saving. The current setting of `0` disables APST outright and parks the drive in ps0 permanently (`APSTE: Disabled`, `PS: 0`), where both healthy nodes report `APSTE: Enabled`.

This is also **stricter than stock**. The kernel's own 100000 default would permit ps5, whose 176 ms entry latency makes it the likeliest thing to have been hanging the drive.

## What changed

- `roles/common/defaults/main.yml`: new, `kernel_cmdline_extra: []`.
- `roles/common/tasks/main.yml`: reset `/etc/default/grub` to the stock empty value on every node, then write `/etc/default/grub.d/99-kernel-cmdline.cfg` with the per-host list. Appends rather than assigns, matching `kdump-tools.cfg`, so `crashkernel=` survives. Always written, so clearing the variable reverts a node instead of stranding its last value.
- `roles/common/handlers/main.yml`: `update-grub`. No reboot, deliberately.
- `host_vars/worker-02.yml`: the one exception, with the power-state table in the comment.

## Verification

`just provision-common` applied clean: `changed=3` on worker-02, `changed=2` on the others, zero failures, and a third run is idempotent.

```
worker-00/01  grub.d: "$GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT "
worker-02     grub.d: "$GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=5000"

worker-02 next boot: ... ro nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=5000 crashkernel=...
worker-02 running:   nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 pcie_aspm=off pcie_port_pm=off
```

## Before rebooting worker-02

Nothing takes effect until a reboot, and this role will not take an etcd member down to get one.

1. **The Tailscale subnet router runs on worker-02** (`ts-homelab-subnet-cnddn-0` and the operator). A reboot cuts remote access to `192.168.30.0/24` until it reschedules.
2. **A kernel update is pending.** Next boot is `7.0.0-29-generic` against `-28` running, so the reboot moves two variables at once.
3. **Rollback:** set `kernel_cmdline_extra` back to `nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0`, re-run `just provision-common`, reboot. That value has 16 days of proven uptime; `5000` has none.

Post-reboot checks: `nvme get-feature -f 0x0c /dev/nvme0 -H` should read `APSTE: Enabled`, and the NVMe hwmon temperature should fall a few degrees from its 60.9 °C p50 (worker-00 and worker-01 sit at 53.9 and 54.9).

## Out of scope

This started as an investigation into worker-02 running about 8 °C hotter than the other two nodes, and it does not fix that. The CPU package sits at a 58 °C median against 50 and 51 while carrying the *lowest* load in the cluster (7% busy, versus 25% on worker-00). The cause is separate: `intel_idle` has no native table for this Comet Lake part, falls back to ACPI `_CST`, and gets only three states.

```
worker-00 (i3-8100T):  C1 C1E C3 C6 C7s C8 C9 C10
worker-02 (i5-10500T): C1_ACPI C2_ACPI C3_ACPI
```

Cores capped at C3 mean the package never reaches PC6 or below, which turbostat confirms: 7.21 W in cores at 5.68% busy, against worker-01's 2.86 W at 9.26% busy. No kernel parameter fixes that. The lever is the BIOS idle power settings, which needs physical access.

author: ekenheim
body:
A cron job repointed at a slower model started failing with:

```
RuntimeError: Non-streaming API call timed out after 90s with no response (threshold: 90s)
```

## This is a misclassification, not a tuning problem

That 90s is Hermes' time-to-first-byte watchdog for **cloud** providers. It isn't supposed to apply to us at all — for local endpoints Hermes disables the watchdog outright (`run_agent.py`, `_resolved_api_call_stale_timeout_base`):

```python
if uses_implicit_default and is_local_endpoint(base_url):
    return float("inf")
```

But `is_local_endpoint` (`agent/model_metadata.py:886`) only recognises loopback, RFC-1918/CGNAT literals, and hostnames with **no dot**:

```python
# Unqualified hostnames (no dots) are local by definition
if host and "." not in host:
    return True
```

`litellm.datasci` has a dot and isn't an IP literal, so our in-cluster proxy is treated as a remote cloud provider and inherits the cloud default.

## Why `stale_timeout_seconds` rather than the tempting one-liner

Shortening `base_url` to `http://litellm:4000` would also satisfy the check — same namespace, identical resolution — but it buys an **infinite** watchdog, so a genuinely dead connection would hang the agent forever. Bounded is better.

`stale_timeout_seconds` is priority 1 in the resolver, above the env var and the default. Being explicit also takes the local-endpoint branch out of play entirely (it only applies to the implicit default), so we stop depending on a hostname-shape heuristic.

## Why 900

`streaming.enabled` is false, so this is a **whole-call budget**, not an idle timer — nothing returns until generation finishes. Sized against measured throughput:

| alias | model | measured | 2k-token answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| `deep` | Qwen3.8-27B (dense) | 8-9 t/s | ~4 min, before prompt processing |
| `self-hosted` | Ornith-1.0-35B | 50.5 t/s idle, ~24 t/s busy | ~85s+ |

90s couldn't cover either. 900 also sits deliberately **above** LiteLLM's own `request_timeout: 600`, so the ceiling is enforced in exactly one place: LiteLLM gives up at 600 and returns a real error, and this watchdog only ever catches a truly dead connection rather than racing its own upstream.

Hermes scales its own floor for large contexts (240s over 100k tokens, 150s over 50k) but never above an explicit setting, so this wins.

## Why it had to be a repo change

`merge-config.py` renders `/opt/data/config.yaml` from this ConfigMap on every start, and the ConfigMap wins:

> Everything in the ConfigMap wins, except that MCP servers present only on the PVC are carried over. That keeps this repo authoritative for the tuning knobs.

Editing the file on the PVC through code-server would work until the next pod restart and then silently revert.

body:
This pull request primarily removes or refactors a significant number of tests and test-only code across multiple modules. The changes aim to clean up unused or redundant tests, reduce the scope of public test helpers, and streamline the types used for deserializing GitHub responses to improve maintainability.

**Test code removal and refactoring:**
* Removed many unit tests and test-only helper functions across modules such as `src/browser.rs`, `src/cache/storage.rs`, `src/cache/tests.rs`, `src/cmd/prune.rs`, `src/cmd/revoke.rs`, `src/token/cleanup.rs`, `src/token/run.rs`, and `src/token/tests.rs`, focusing on tests that were redundant, covered elsewhere, or no longer relevant after recent changes. * Renamed and clarified several test function names to better reflect their purpose, e.g., `cache_entry_json_format_is_compatible` to `current_cache_schema_is_stable_and_round_trips`, and improved assertions for more robust round-trip testing.

**Data structure simplification:**
* Simplified GitHub API response types in `src/github/types.rs` by removing unused fields and unnecessary derives (e.g., `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Serialize`), and removing the `RepositoryInfo` type. This reduces coupling to the external API and makes the codebase easier to maintain.

**Test coverage and error handling improvements:**
* Improved error handling in test writers, ensuring that output write failures are reported with the correct error kind (`BrokenPipe`).
* Added additional test cases for schema compatibility and unsupported schema handling in cache logic.

**Command-line interface adjustments:**
* Updated CLI tests in `src/cmd.rs` to reflect the removal of deprecated commands, ensuring only current commands are tested.

author: ohah
body:
## 의도

SSH 클라이언트 계획의 **S4b — 전송 루프**다. S4 까지로 패킷 하나를 봉인하고 풀 수 있게 됐지만, **그 층들은 연결 전체의 상태를 모른다**:

- `packet.zig`·`cipher.zig` 는 패킷 **하나**를 안다. 시퀀스 번호는 연결 전체의 상태다.
- 평문 구간과 암호 구간은 프레이밍이 다른데, 그 전환점(`NEWKEYS`)이 **방향마다 따로** 온다.
- strict KEX 의 요구 넷 중 둘은 **"지금까지 무엇을 받았나" 를 기억해야** 판정되는 사후 검사다.

이 층이 그 셋을 든다. 여전히 sans-io 다 — 선에서 온 바이트를 받아 패킷 하나를 꺼내고, payload 를 받아 보낼 바이트를 만든다.

## 구현

새 파일 하나(`src/session/ssh/transport.zig`)와 배럴 등록(`src/session.zig` 의 `ssh.transport`)이다.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> initial_kex
    initial_kex --> initial_kex: "feed() — KEX 메시지만 허용 (draft §3.2)"
    initial_kex --> established: "enableSendKeys + enableRecvKeys 둘 다"
    established --> established: "feed() — 모든 메시지 허용"
    note right of initial_kex
        recv_seq +%= 1 은 무엇을 하든 먼저 돈다
        (버려도·끊어도 받은 것은 받은 것)
    end note
    note right of established
        NEWKEYS 는 옛 키로 나가고
        그 직후 enable*Keys 가 교체 + 리셋
    end note
```

### 타입과 함수

- **`Transport`** — `send_seq`/`recv_seq`(방향별), `send_cipher`/`recv_cipher`(`null` 이면 평문 프레이밍), `strict_kex`, `phase`, `got_first_from_peer`, `pending_discard`, `seen_kexinit`/`seen_ecdh_reply`.
- **`send(out, payload, rand)`** — 현재 프레이밍으로 봉인하고 `send_seq` 를 올린다. `NEWKEYS` 도 그냥 부르면 된다(그 패킷은 **옛 키로** 나가야 한다).
- **`sendLen(payload_len)`** — 버퍼를 잡기 전에 크기를 묻는다(프레이밍에 따라 다르다).
- **`feed(out, buf) → ?Received`** — 덜 왔으면 `null`(오류가 아니라 상태). 꺼냈으면 payload·consumed·**그 패킷의 seq** 를 준다(`SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED` 로 되돌려 줄 때 쓴다, draft §3.3).
- **`enableSendKeys` / `enableRecvKeys`** — `NEWKEYS` 를 보낸/받은 **직후** 부른다. 옛 키를 `clear()` 하고 새 키를 걸고, strict KEX 면 **자기 방향 번호만** 0 으로 리셋한다.
- **`clear()`** — 연결 종료 시 양쪽 키 소거.

### 순서가 곧 계약인 자리 셋

1. **번호는 무엇을 하든 먼저 오른다.** 버리는 추측 패킷(RFC 4253 §7.1)도, §3.2 위반으로 끊는 패킷도 이미 받은 것이다. `feed` 는 `recv_seq +%= 1` 을 **판정보다 먼저** 한다 — 하나만 빠뜨리면 그 뒤 모든 AEAD 태그가 어긋나고, 증상은 KEX 가 아니라 한참 뒤 채널 데이터에서 나온다.
2. **`NEWKEYS` 는 옛 키로 보내고 그 직후에 바꾼다**(RFC 4253 §7.3). 전환이 먼저 일어나면 서버가 그 패킷을 못 읽는다. 그래서 교체는 `send` 안이 아니라 **호출자가 부르는 별도 함수**다.
3. **버리기가 §3.2 검사보다 먼저**다. 버릴 패킷은 KEX 메시지가 아닐 수 있는데, 순서가 반대면 버려야 할 것을 위반으로 읽어 연결을 끊는다.

### strict KEX 수신 게이트 넷 (draft §3.2)

| 요구 | 어떻게 | 왜 사후 검사인가 |
|---|---|---|
| KEX 메시지만 받는다 | `isKexMessage` 허용 목록 | — |
| 첫 메시지가 KEXINIT | `got_first_from_peer` 를 들고 한 번만 본다 | 이미 지나간 패킷을 되짚어야 한다 |
| 번호 wrap 금지 | `recv_seq == 0` 으로 감싸 돌았는지 본다 | 올린 **뒤에** 판정해야 안다 |
| 정해진 횟수만 | `seen_kexinit`·`seen_ecdh_reply` | 누적을 기억해야 한다 |

`NEWKEYS` 는 계수 대상이 아니다 — 재키잉마다 다시 온다.

## 문서 정합성

- **[docs/ssh-client.md](../blob/main/docs/ssh-client.md) §4.4 신설** — "전송 루프가 드는 것". 위 다섯 규칙을 계약으로 못박았다. 특히 **양쪽 키가 다 붙어야 초기 KEX 가 끝난다**는 것과 그것을 한쪽에서만 판정하면 무슨 일이 나는지를 적었다(아래 "검증에서 잡은 것").
- **[docs/plans/ssh-client.md](../blob/main/docs/plans/ssh-client.md)** — S4b 행을 실제로 한 것으로 채웠다.

## clean-room 근거

**공개 명세 유도**다. 레퍼런스 구현 소스는 읽지 않았다.

- [draft-ietf-sshm-strict-kex](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-sshm-strict-kex/) §3.2(허용 메시지 목록·첫 메시지 검사·wrap 금지·횟수 제한), §3.3(`NEWKEYS` 뒤 번호 리셋과 그 시점, `SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED` 의 번호 처리).
- [RFC 4253](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4253.txt) §7.1(추측 패킷 폐기), §7.3(`NEWKEYS` 는 옛 키로 보낸다), §12(메시지 번호).
- [RFC 5656](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5656.txt) §7.1(ECDH 메시지 번호 30·31).

사실상 표준 항목 없음.

## 전략 영향 평가

충돌 없다. 계층 규칙(L2 sans-io)도 그대로이고 `tests/boundary/ssh_sans_io.zig` 가 이 파일도 등록 없이 자동 검사한다.

## 테스트

```
$ zig test src/session/ssh/transport.zig
All 40 tests passed.          # transport 14 + cipher/packet(의존 모듈)

$ zig test tests/boundary/ssh_sans_io.zig
All 5 tests passed.

$ mise run check
[test] 3581 passed; 53 skipped; 0 failed.
[test] 2771 passed;  2 skipped; 0 failed.
[test] 2265 passed; 29 skipped; 0 failed.
[test] 1463 passed;  7 skipped; 0 failed.
[test] 1429 passed;  7 skipped; 0 failed.
[check-boundaries] 전부 통과
```

`mise run check` 는 `src/platform/windows/{d3d11,dwrite_font,win32_window}.zig` 의 `calling convention 'aarch64_aapcs_win' not supported` 로 exit 1 인데 **이 PR 과 무관한 기존 실패**다(macOS ARM 로컬 전용, CI 는 ubuntu 에서 돈다). `git diff origin/main --stat` 에 그 파일들이 없다.

### 변이 검사 (22/22 죽음)

| 무엇을 망가뜨렸나 | 잡은 테스트 |
|---|---|
| `send_seq`/`recv_seq` 안 오름 | 방향별 계수 · 양방향 왕복 |
| 버린 패킷은 안 셈 | 추측 패킷 폐기 |
| strict 아닌데 리셋 / strict 인데 리셋 안 함(양방향) | `NEWKEYS` 전환 · 받는 번호 리셋 |
| `recv` 리셋을 `send` 쪽에 | 받는 번호 리셋 |
| 첫 메시지 검사 삭제 / strict 무관하게 적용 | 첫 메시지 KEXINIT |
| KEX 게이트 삭제 / strict 무관하게 적용 | 초기 KEX 중 비-KEX 거절 |
| `isKexMessage` 에 `IGNORE`·`DEBUG` 추가 | 같은 테스트(그 둘이 정확히 Terrapin 의 도구다) |
| 중복 계수 삭제 | 같은 KEX 메시지 두 번 |
| wrap 검사 삭제 | 번호 wrap |
| 폐기를 안 함 / 계속 함 | 추측 패킷 폐기 |
| 암호 구간인데 평문으로 읽기 / 쓰기 | 양방향 왕복 · 덜 온 바이트 |
| `send` 만 phase 판정 | established 순서 무관(아래) |

### 검증에서 잡은 것 둘

1. **`enableSendKeys` 가 phase 를 판정하지 않았다.** `NEWKEYS` 를 주고받는 순서는 정해져 있지 않은데 받는 쪽에서만 판정해서, **"받고 나서 보낸" 연결이 영원히 초기 KEX 에 갇힌다** — 그러면 이후 정상 트래픽(`SSH_MSG_IGNORE`·채널 데이터)이 전부 §3.2 위반으로 끊긴다. 두 순서를 다 재고, 그 **관측 가능한 결과**(established 뒤 `CHANNEL_DATA` 가 통과하는지)까지 못박았다.
2. **`recv_seq` 리셋을 지워도 아무 테스트가 안 잡았다.** 테스트가 0 에서 시작해 0 을 확인하니 실은 아무것도 안 쟀던 것이다. 평문 구간에서 번호를 3 까지 올려 둔 뒤 리셋을 재고, **상대가 0 번으로 봉인한 패킷이 실제로 풀리는지**까지 확인하도록 고쳤다 — 번호만 보면 "왜 0 이어야 하는지" 가 안 남는다.

## E2E/관측 가능성

순수 상태기계라 아티팩트가 없다 — 그게 sans-io 로 짠 이유다. 관측 경로는 단위 테스트와 변이 검사이고, 실서버 왕복은 S8 이 든다.

## 한계

- **KEX 를 실제로 진행하지 않는다.** 이 층은 "무엇을 받았고 번호가 몇인가" 만 안다 — KEXINIT 협상(S2)·KEX 계산(S3)·키 유도의 결과를 **호출자가 넣어 준다**(`enable*Keys`·`pending_discard`·`strict_kex`). 그 조립이 아직 없다(S8).
- **재키잉을 상태로 표현하지 않는다.** 재키잉은 `established` 에서 KEXINIT 을 주고받고 다시 `enable*Keys` 를 부르는 것으로 처리된다 — draft §3.2 의 제한은 **초기 KEX 에만** 걸리므로 그것으로 충분하지만, "재키잉 중"이라는 별도 상태가 없어 그 사이 채널 데이터를 막지는 않는다. RFC 4253 §7.1 이 요구하는 "KEX 중 일부 메시지 금지"는 **초기 KEX 밖에서는 우리가 안 건다**.
- **`SSH_MSG_UNIMPLEMENTED` 를 보내지 않는다.** `Received.seq` 로 재료는 주지만 실제 응답은 S7c 의 몫이다.
- **부분 패킷을 버퍼링하지 않는다.** `feed` 는 호출자의 누적 버퍼를 매번 다시 본다 — 암호 구간에서는 길이 필드를 매 호출 복호하므로 조각이 많이 오면 그만큼 반복한다. 터미널 트래픽 규모에서 문제될 양이 아니라고 봤고, 문제가 되면 길이 복호 결과를 캐시하면 된다.
- **실서버에 붙여 본 적이 없다.** 순서 규칙은 명세를 읽은 대로 짰고, 그 조립의 증명은 S8 이다.

## 사용자 논의 필요 여부

**없다.** 전부 명세의 MUST 를 옮긴 것이고, 계약 §4.4 에 그대로 적었다.

author: artyhoo
body:
## What this is

A **decision brief**, not a build order — and it opens by retracting the observation that
spawned it.

PR #1444's backward sweep (T21) named the kickoff `host-verify` contract as a sibling of the
ask-file gap it had just closed: same shape — hand-authored format, gate present
(`.claude/hooks/check-kickoff-traps.sh:132`), reader present (`scripts/host-verify.sh --list`,
usage at `:60`), **emitter absent**. That observation was recorded on *shape*, before any
measurement. The measurement has now been taken and it does not support building.

## The measurement (host, 2026-08-17)

| Question | Result |
|---|---|
| tracked kickoffs | **310** |
| …carrying a `host-verify` contract | **42** |
| …carrying the `host-verify: none` opt-out | **13** |
| …carrying neither | **258** |
| of the 42 contracts, **failing to parse** through the real runner | **0** |

The last row is load-bearing. The hypothesis behind the observation — *"with no emitter,
authors write the contract wrong"* — is **falsified at full coverage** of the contract-carrying
population, not on a sample.

The 258 are **not** a backlog: arm 1 is forward-going and
[`destination-environment-verification.md §6`](.claude/rules/destination-environment-verification.md)
says so in its own honest-limit paragraph. The opt-out population was checked for
`#optout-as-reflex` and came back healthy — substantive rationales, and one kickoff even
retracts its own earlier opt-out as wrong. The single suspicious string `host-verify: none - no`
is a **negative test-case row in a table** (`autonomy-mechanisms-hardening/kickoff.md:90`), not a
live opt-out; that file's real contract parses.

## Why the ask file needed its emitter and this does not

The difference is the **worked-example population**, and it is the whole argument:

- **Ask file before #1444:** zero instances existed anywhere — empty mailbox, no ask ever filed,
  schema stated only inside the checker. The first author had nothing to copy.
- **`host-verify` today:** 42 working, parsing instances sit beside every kickoff an author is
  already reading. **The corpus is the template.**

Against [`effort-worthiness.md §1`](.claude/rules/effort-worthiness.md)'s four-test card it fails
test 3 hardest — immaterial, at 0 measured defects. Recommendation: **DON'T BUILD**, with four
concrete falsifiers in §3 that would overturn it (a malformed contract reaching a merged kickoff;
the corpus becoming unreachable on the shipped axis, e.g. consumer kickoffs landing in
`.ai-factory/` with no examples beside them; a grammar change turning 42 examples stale; ≥3
`#optout-as-reflex` incidents).

## Two traps named because both are live

- **T-HV-A** — transferring a fresh, satisfying fix to a shape-alike whose *problem class*
  differs. This is T16 `#pattern-matching-on-name` one level up: at the level of a remedy rather
  than a tool.
- **T-HV-B** — reading the 258 contract-less kickoffs as a backlog. A large, impressive, entirely
  fake number, and exactly what a session under mild pressure to produce findings will reach for.

## Method note (carried into the brief, because the first run was wrong)

The Bash tool here is **zsh**, where `for f in $VAR` does **not** word-split. A 310-line file
list was consumed as one word and the first counts came back `neither=1` against
`contract=40, optout=13` — incoherent, which is what exposed it. Re-measurement must iterate with
`while IFS= read -r`. The numbers above are the corrected run.

## Self-application

The brief argues the contract format is learnable from its corpus, so it carries a contract
written that way — and the real runner executes it on the host:

```
$ bash scripts/host-verify.sh host-verify-authoring-half
── host-verify result: 3/3 passed on Darwin
✅ host-verify passed
```

Principle 12 (T-enumeration) and the 600-line markdown gate both pass (184 lines).

## Scope

One new markdown dispatch input; nothing else touched. Deliberately **not** appended to #1444 —
different concern, and #1444 was already green and reviewed (CLAUDE.md `PR strategy`).

Prior-art: skipped — documentation only, no capability: one markdown file, no dependency, no module, nothing under `packages/`.

## Fidelity verdict

FIDELITY: skipped — not a stage PR; no dispatched substrate and no `## Provenance` section, so there is no kickoff-vs-diff boundary for a cold auditor to adjudicate. This PR's own acceptance is the host-verify run quoted above.

## §1.7 self-reflexive sections

### §1.7 Forward-check applied

Complies with [`effort-worthiness.md §1`](.claude/rules/effort-worthiness.md) in the strongest
available sense: this PR *is* the four-test card run against a proposal, and it returns the
answer the rule explicitly legitimises — «„not worth it" verdicts are legitimate outcomes». The
burden of proof sat on *more* rigor and was not discharged, so the default (practice-first,
build nothing) stands.

Complies with [`no-paid-llm-in-ci.md`](.claude/rules/no-paid-llm-in-ci.md): every number in the
brief comes from deterministic `git ls-files` / `grep` / `host-verify.sh` runs — zero API-billed
calls, and each is re-runnable from the contract block at
`.claude/orchestrator-prompts/host-verify-authoring-half/kickoff.md:170`.

Complies with [`destination-environment-verification.md §1`](.claude/rules/destination-environment-verification.md):
the brief carries a real `host-verify` contract, not an opt-out, and it was *executed* on the
host (3/3 on Darwin) rather than merely declared — which matters doubly here, since the brief's
subject is that contract format.

Complies with [`ai-laziness-traps.md §3`](.claude/rules/ai-laziness-traps.md) kickoff-author
obligations: T-numbers enumerated (T2/T3/T14/T18/T20/T21) rather than blanket-referenced, plus
two domain traps. **T14 in particular is applied rather than cited**: the sweep came back clean
at *full* coverage of the contract-carrying population (42/42), which is what licenses reading it
as «category clean» instead of «coverage insufficient to conclude».

Complies with [`kickoff-staging-placement.md §1`](.claude/rules/kickoff-staging-placement.md):
this is a tracked dispatch input and must reach `staging` before any session is pointed at it —
stated in the handoff rather than assumed.

Complies with [`language-discipline.md §1`](.claude/rules/language-discipline.md) (repo artefacts
in English) and [`build-first-reuse-default.md`](.claude/rules/build-first-reuse-default.md)
(**no capability at all** — the verdict is to build nothing; one markdown file, no dependency, no
module, nothing under `packages/`).

### §1.7 Backward-check applied

**Class of this change** = *a T21 backward-sweep observation that names a sibling surface and
proposes a mechanism, recorded on shape before any measurement.*

Surfaces where class-X occurs, enumerated outward from this PR rather than from its own diff:

- **PR #1444 observation 2** (`.claude/orchestrator-prompts/host-verify-authoring-half/kickoff.md:14`)
  — **GAP-FOUND then RETRACTED.** This PR is that measurement. The shape claim was true; the
  harm claim was false at 42/42.
- **PR #1444 observations 1 and 3** — **SWEPT, out of class.** Neither proposes a mechanism:
  observation 1 is a one-line pointer into
  [`reviewer-discipline.md:65`](.claude/rules/reviewer-discipline.md) and observation 3 is a
  stale-label fact about [`effort-worthiness.md:62-64`](.claude/rules/effort-worthiness.md).
  Both are carried into the brief's §4 as maintainer-owned items rather than silently actioned.
- **[`ai-laziness-traps.md §2 T21`](.claude/rules/ai-laziness-traps.md)** — **SWEPT-CLEAN, not
  edited.** T21 prescribes delegating the sweep to a cold agent precisely so a sweep cannot
  become a restatement; it says nothing about measuring a *surviving* observation before acting
  on it. This PR is an instance of the gap being real and the remedy being wrong, which is
  within T21's intent, so no amendment is proposed and none is smuggled in.

author: danieljvdm
body:
## Summary

- A human can dispatch **one** inline review comment as a work order: a reply whose body is exactly `@effect-agent fix this` and whose `in_reply_to` names that comment, or a configured reaction on it. The transport must prove the target; a conversation comment, review summary, mention without `in_reply_to`, fork, foreign repo, stale comment head, or unauthorized actor id is rejected before the implementer runs.
- This is the GitHub-facing follow-up to the class E [work-order host](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/docs/spec/pr-work-orders.md). The host still owns the jailed implementer. Ingress owns authentication, work-order construction, durable admission, isolated publication, and a host-authored thread reply that never resolves the thread.
- `@effect-agent/pr-review` stays read-only. No GitHub workflow is enabled.

## Architecture

One accepted delivery becomes one work order, then one host attempt.

1. **Authenticate** the webhook HMAC or Actions identity, then parse a unique inline target from the event. See [delivery authentication](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/src/authenticate.ts) and [event targeting](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/src/parse-event.ts).
2. **Authorize and construct** the canonical work order from the GitHub comment and current PR head: stable actor id (not login), same-repository non-fork, `source.commitSha === headSha`. See [work-order construction](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/src/construct.ts).
3. **Claim** `(repository, pullRequestNumber, headSha, workOrderId)` on a file-backed store. Duplicate `eventId` returns the stored outcome. A crash after claim and before a stored outcome is a typed incomplete settlement and is not retried. See the [durable attempt store](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/src/store.ts).
4. **Invoke the existing host** (`runWorkOrder`) rather than widening implementer authority. See the [ingress orchestrator](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/src/ingress.ts).
5. **Publish** only through an isolated publisher that re-verifies digest, allowlisted paths, required-check evidence, work-order identity, and expected head, then compare-and-swaps. A lost race is `StalePullRequestHead`. See the [isolated publisher](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/src/publisher.ts).
6. **Present** one host-authored reply (`published` / `settled` / `failed`). The source thread stays open. See [thread presentation](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/src/presentation.ts).

Normative spec: [pull-request work-order ingress](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/docs/spec/pr-work-order-ingress.md).

## Evidence

The private leaf suite in [`examples/pr-work-order-ingress/test/pr-work-order-ingress.test.ts`](https://github.com/danieljvdm/effect-agent/blob/edcbadf56d79a9c6e7f29d232b95f6493bd40a5a/examples/pr-work-order-ingress/test/pr-work-order-ingress.test.ts) uses recorded event fixtures and a fake GitHub API (no live network):

- mention reply with `in_reply_to` and reaction each construct one work order and invoke the host once
- mention without a unique inline target, PR conversation comment, review summary, and pathless event are rejected
- unauthorized actor id is rejected even when the login matches
- fork, foreign repository, and stale comment head are rejected
- duplicate `eventId` returns the stored outcome; a second dispatch gets a new work-order id
- a crash after claim records `AttemptIncomplete` and does not retry
- the check process environment contains neither a GitHub write token nor a model secret
- the publisher rejects digest, path, and head mismatches and does not update the ref
- published/settled runs post one thread reply and never resolve the thread

author: dave3130
body:
## AIR-606 — Release Readiness Report Generation Issue

**Problem:** the rca-build skill's final step called `triggerRcaReport(buildUuid)` without `force`. With `force=false` the endpoint returns an existing (possibly stale/empty) report via the fast-path, or effectively waits on a full/bulk RCA of every test — so the release-readiness report did not reliably reflect this run's analysis, and could appear "not generated" post-analysis.

**Fix:** always call `triggerRcaReport(buildUuid=<build id>, force=true)` in Step 6; never `force=false`. Forcing regenerates the report from the RCAs completed so far, so it is produced for this run even when only a subset of tests reached terminal RCA — instead of returning a cached report or blocking on a bulk re-trigger of every test's RCA.

### Change
- `skills/rca-build/SKILL.md` Step 6 — the report trigger now mandates `force=true`, with rationale.

### Testing
- **Manually verified on a prod build via the MCP flow** with `force=true`: the release-readiness report is generated from the completed RCAs even when only a partial number of tests have terminal RCA — no bulk-trigger-and-wait needed.

Targets `feat/generic-rca-agent-plugin-v3`.

author: sarder-abedin
body:
Makes running the server **natively** a single command — nicer than Docker while iterating (config/code changes take effect on restart, logs + the HF model cache are just local files, GPU access needs no device flags).

## How the AI models install
Two layers, only one is pip:
- **Frameworks (pip):** `torch`, `transformers`, `ultralytics`, … — the code that runs the models.
- **Model weights (NOT pip):** `transformers`/`ultralytics` **auto-download** them from HuggingFace on the first live run and cache them (`~/.cache/huggingface`, `./yolo11n.pt`). No install step; offline → stubs.

## What's added / changed
- **`start.sh`** (repo root) — one command. First run: venv + deps, **auto-picking ROCm torch** when a Radeon is present (`/dev/kfd`) else CPU/CUDA. Every run: launches the AI server (YOLO + V-JEPA 2 + SSv2 + depth, all in `main_server.py`) **and** the PyQt viewer (world map + foresight) together, clean joint shutdown (`wait -n` + trap). Flags: `--demo`, `--nav baseline`, `--no-ui`, `--cpu`, `--setup`; env `NAV_MODE`/`NAV_STRATEGY`/`ROCM_INDEX`. Sets `QT_QPA_PLATFORM=wayland` on a Wayland session. (Docker still uses `start_server.sh`.)
- **`requirements-rocm.txt`** — one-shot ROCm dep set (headless opencv). torch is intentionally **not** listed (installed from the ROCm index first so PyPI's newer CPU/CUDA wheel can't override the GPU build); the header documents the manual two-line install.
- **Docs (careful pass):** README "How" + first-run checklist gain the `./start.sh` path; `HOW_TO_RUN.md` §2 presents native (§2.2) vs Docker (§2.1), and §2.3 AMD points at `./start.sh` (auto) and `requirements-rocm.txt` (manual, torch-first).

## Usage
```bash
./start.sh                 # first run: setup + live server + PyQt viewer
./start.sh --demo          # demo mode · --nav baseline · --no-ui · --setup (reinstall)
```

## Testing
Docs + scripts only — no Python changed. `start.sh` `bash -n` clean, `--help`/arg-parsing smoke-tested; README/HOW_TO_RUN fences balanced and cross-refs consistent. Full test suite **341 passed** (only the pre-existing `torch`-missing `world_model` tests fail).

author: sebastianschuetze
body:
## Aktueller Stand

GitHub kann verwaltete Issue-, Project- und Beziehungsänderungen jetzt an FounderOps melden. FounderOps bleibt die erste Wahrheit: Eine GitHub-Änderung wird nur übernommen, wenn die auslösende Person in FounderOps zugeordnet und für genau diesen Prozess berechtigt ist.

## Problem

Der bisherige Webhook-Weg konnte Lieferungen sicher annehmen und protokollieren, setzte aber den FounderOps-Schreibvertrag noch nicht vollständig durch. Ohne kausale Actor- und Versionsprüfung konnten verzögerte Events, Project-Snapshots oder repositoryübergreifende Beziehungen zu Drift führen. Review- und abgeschlossene Items mussten außerdem auch über GitHub gegen unzulässige Änderungen geschützt werden.

## Änderung

- autorisierte GitHub-Änderungen werden im selben Prozess in FounderOps ausgeführt
- nicht erlaubte, nicht zuordenbare oder veraltete Änderungen werden sofort mit der FounderOps-App-Identität zurückgeschrieben
- Review- und abgeschlossene Items bleiben für fachliche Änderungen gesperrt; Kommentare bleiben erlaubt
- Issue-, Project-v2- und Sub-Issue/Dependency-Events verwenden stabile Actor-, Repository- und Versionsidentitäten
- Projektions-Outbox, Retry, Terminalfehler und Wartungsworkflow bilden einen gemeinsamen verlässlichen Abschluss
- repositoryübergreifende Dependencies unterscheiden Repository und Issue-Nummer
- GitHub-App- und Organization-Webhook-Aktivierung sind getrennt dokumentiert
- kein Product Update: rein operativer Integrations- und Schutzvertrag ohne neue UI-Funktion

## Wirkung

GitHub bleibt ein Arbeitskanal, kann FounderOps-Prozessregeln aber nicht umgehen. Erlaubte Änderungen erscheinen direkt in FounderOps; unerlaubte Änderungen werden ohne manuellen späteren Sync korrigiert.

author: richardroberthackerworld-rgb
body:
## Scope, first

This is the whole of `hand-engine`'s divergence from `main`: **248 commits, 387 files**, spanning `android/`, `7marks/`, `blog/`, `7solve/`, `videotools/`, `hand/`, `account-hub/`, `pay/` and more. It is not a review-in-one-sitting PR. Most of it landed in earlier sessions; the section below covers only the most recent work, on 7Solve.

## 7Solve — verification became a gate, not a badge

The answer page used to ask the student what they were studying, then answer in fourteen mandated sections behind a Contents rail. Both are gone. The study profile is now read out of the question itself, and the default answer is:

> Final Answer → Method → Step-by-Step → Verification → Final Result

with optional sections only when the question earns them. The prompt says as much in as many words: an answer padded with generic sections is a worse answer.

### Why the checker had to be rebuilt

A reported answer claimed `(5,3)` solves `x² + y² + 1 = 3xy`. It does not — 35 ≠ 45 — and nothing in the product noticed, because the equation reader was a regex that rejected any letter but `x`. A two-variable question produced **zero checks**.

It is now a tokeniser and recursive-descent parser over multivariate expressions, which is what makes the rest possible:

- claimed solutions substituted back into the original question
- claimed transformations applied to independently-found solutions and **iterated** (the reported `(x,y) → (3y−x, x)` works once from (2,1), which is how it survived review)
- exact forms evaluated, so `82 − 30√7` verifies and `√25200 = 60√7` holds
- completeness enumerated, so "n = 3" is refuted by n = 1, 2, 4, 5
- divisibility, chemical balancing, units, probability bounds

When a proof-tier check fails, the answer is **not shown**: it returns to the model with the failing checks and is re-solved once, sharing one idempotency id so our own rejection is never billed to the student.

### Two rules that run through all of it

**A heuristic never outranks a proof.** Only a failed proof yields "✗ Verification failed"; a failed hint downgrades to "⚠ Partially verified" and stays visible. A checker that cries wolf gets ignored, and an ignored checker is worse than none.

**Nothing claims a check that did not happen.** The "Checked ✓" stamp used to print on every answer regardless of whether anything was checked. It is now written from the real result and left blank when there is nothing to say.

## Also in this branch

- **Credits**: read-then-write races closed under one lock; `?action=charge` is idempotent, so a retry on mobile data cannot spend twice
- **Exam mode**: a real paper — question palette, negative marking, autosave that survives a closed tab, no answers until submit
- **Sandbox**: JavaScript and Python (Pyodide) genuinely execute, sealed from the network; C/C++/Java say plainly that they cannot
- **Live sources** with authority tiers, behind an SSRF guard tested against userinfo smuggling (`https://evil.com@127.0.0.1/`) and suffix spoofing (`gov.in.evil.com`)
- **Feedback loop** and an admin quality dashboard, off until `admin_token` is set to ≥16 chars
- **Model map**, which had rotted: `gemini-2.5-flash`, `cerebras llama-3.3-70b`, every OpenRouter `:free` model and GitHub Models were all returning 404/410 — the live site was walking dead engines
- **Router**: a 429 from one provider no longer aborts the whole chain. Gemini's quota is not Groq's quota.

## Testing

- **99-case verification suite**, all passing, shipped inside the build and runnable from Settings on the live site
- **Live-tested across 15 question types.** Four faults were found by that testing — three false positives in the checker and the 429 abort — all fixed
- The nine cases that passed *before* those fixes were **re-run afterwards; none regressed**
- Desktop 1280/1440 and mobile 375px; no horizontal overflow; 21 views mount with zero console errors

## Known limitations

- Identity checking is numerical (12 random points, variables varied independently), not symbolic — conclusive against wrong claims, strong evidence for right ones, never reported as proof
- Completeness search is bounded; absence of counterexamples is reported as exactly that
- No pronoun resolution: "so n²+n+1 divides **it**" yields no verdict rather than a wrong one
- The 4,000-question benchmark from the brief is not built — it needs trusted expected answers, which is a sourcing project, and fabricating them would defeat the point

author: jman730
body:
Follow-up to #188. Fixes #171.

## The fix in #188 is right, and it is also version-dependent

#188 removed the `timedelta(...)` wrappers and passed `read_timeout_seconds` as a raw float. For the SDK release the reporter of #171 was running, that is correct: the value reached `anyio.fail_after()`, which computes `current_time() + delay`, so a `timedelta` produced

```
TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'float' and 'datetime.timedelta'
```

On current releases the parameter has the opposite contract. Checked against `mcp` 1.28.1:

```python
# mcp/client/session.py
read_timeout_seconds: datetime.timedelta | None = None

# mcp/shared/session.py:286-288
if request_read_timeout_seconds is not None:
    timeout = request_read_timeout_seconds.total_seconds()
elif self._session_read_timeout_seconds is not None:
    timeout = self._session_read_timeout_seconds.total_seconds()
```

A float there raises `AttributeError: 'float' object has no attribute 'total_seconds'` on the first tool call — the same user-visible symptom #171 describes, from the opposite cause.

`mcp` is not pinned in `pyproject.toml`; it is picked up from whatever the user has installed. So neither the float form nor the `timedelta` form is correct for all installs, and swapping between them just moves the breakage from one half of the userbase to the other. I nearly opened exactly that swap-back PR before checking the installed SDK — closing it in favour of this.

## Approach

Stop passing `read_timeout_seconds` entirely and bound every SDK await with `asyncio.wait_for`, which is the timeout mechanism most call sites already used:

- `lifecycle.py:479` — `call_tool` on the one-shot stdio path, already wrapped with `tool_timeout`
- `lifecycle.py:1650` — `call_tool` in `_call_attached_server`, already wrapped with `tool_timeout`
- `lifecycle.py:535` — `list_tools` on the persistent stdio path, already wrapped
- `_probe_mixin.py:253,260` — both probe coroutines, already wrapped by `_run_probe`

`_async_probe_stdio_server` has always constructed `ClientSession(read_stream, write_stream)` with no SDK timeout, so this makes the layer internally consistent rather than introducing a new convention.

Awaits that had *no* bound before and now have one:

| Site | Bound by |
|---|---|
| `session.initialize()` — one-shot stdio, persistent stdio, persistent HTTP, persistent SSE | `startup_timeout` |
| `session.list_tools()` — persistent HTTP, persistent SSE | `tool_timeout` |

The two `list_tools()` calls sat inside bare `try/except Exception: pass` blocks, so an unresponsive server hung session setup indefinitely with no error — that was latent before this PR and is fixed here.

`sse_read_timeout` on the transport clients still takes a float; that parameter is genuinely typed as seconds and is untouched.

## Blast radius if left as-is

Anyone on an SDK where `read_timeout_seconds` is `timedelta`-typed — which includes current PyPI `mcp` — cannot make a single MCP tool call. The server registers, its tools are advertised to the model, and the first invocation fails with an `AttributeError` that reads as an internal VulnClaw crash rather than a version mismatch.

## Tests

`TestSessionTimeouts` in `tests/mcp/test_mcp_lifecycle.py`:

- `test_no_client_session_passes_read_timeout_seconds` scans `vulnclaw/mcp/*.py` for non-comment `read_timeout_seconds=` and fails on any hit. This is the regression guard that keeps the codebase from oscillating between the two broken forms as the SDK moves.
- `test_attached_server_call_times_out_without_sdk_timeout` drives `_call_attached_server` against a session whose `call_tool` sleeps for 60s with a 10 ms configured `tool_timeout`, and asserts `asyncio.TimeoutError` — proving the local bound is what enforces the timeout now.

```
ruff check vulnclaw tests   # All checks passed
pytest -q                   # 1427 passed, 1 skipped
```

No frontend files are touched.

author: mobeenabdullah
body:
This is the defect behind **"I am not able to create a new single"**. Reproduced in a browser: `POST /admin/api/singles` returned **503** on every attempt.

## What the user saw, and why it was the wrong advice

```
Service unavailable. Please try again later.
```

The real cause reached the server log and nothing else:

```
[Nextly HMR] schema reload skipped: [SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE]
  field-group migration could not take the migration lock; another run holds it
  heldBy: "hmr reload#f2826085-..."
```

A lock table predating `expires_at` grants an **owner-only claim**, and an owner-only claim has **no takeover** — `session.ts` documents this deliberately at `:692`. So a killed process leaves a claim no later run can reclaim, and every schema change refuses until an operator intervenes.

**Retrying never starts succeeding. Restarting the server does not clear it either.** The one thing the message told the caller to do was the one thing that could not work.

## The change

`serviceUnavailable` hardcoded its public message, so no caller could say anything else. It now takes an override and keeps the old text as the default — most causes of an unavailable service genuinely are transient, and "try again later" is right for those.

The lock refusal supplies a message naming the remedy: `nextly migrate:field-groups`, which adds the column and restores takeover.

## Why the message names both causes

This code **cannot tell a concurrently held lock from an abandoned one** — that is the same missing expiry column. Claiming either would be a guess, and naming only the transient cause is exactly what left the retry advice standing. So it states both and lets the operator check which they are in.

## Testing

Three cases in `nextly-error.test.ts`, and the second exists to make the first mean something:

| assertion | why |
|---|---|
| the override reaches `publicMessage` | the behaviour being added |
| the default still applies with no override | **control** — without it, the assertion above is satisfied by a factory that ignores its argument and happens to be called with the default text |
| `code` stays `SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE` | the override changes what a person is told; it must not change what a client branches on |

**Stub-verified:** ignoring the override fails exactly the first test, with the control still passing.

- `packages/nextly` errors + field-group migration suites: **29 files, 589 tests** passing
- `check-types`: **0 errors**

## Inherited failure

`origin/main` is red on `scripts/turbo-inputs.test.mjs` (`expected 23 to be greater than 25` — a hardcoded floor invalidated by a legitimate e2e deletion). Every open PR inherits it; a fix is in flight from another lane. This branch touches no e2e module.

Changeset: `patch`, generated from the `fixed` group and verified.

author: sagarsuperuser
body:
## What

A third, instrumented AWS run (`c7g.2xlarge` + `db.m7g.4xlarge`, 100 GB gp3, PG 16.14) to attribute the latency-tail events the earlier runs could not: 1-second Enhanced Monitoring, Performance Insights, a 5-second single-statement DB sampler (`pg_stat_io`, `pg_stat_wal`, `pg_stat_bgwriter`, vacuum/analyze progress, GIN pending list, page/extension locks, `pg_ls_waldir` pool depth, every backend's wait event) and the Postgres log with the attribution logging on.

**Finding.** The stalls are WAL segment creation under `WALWriteLock` when the pool of pre-made segments runs dry. From `xlog.c` (verified from source): with WAL-driven checkpoints the pool at each completion is ~one checkpoint's worth with less than a segment of margin; after a lull, small checkpoints unlink segments (`min_wal_size` = 192 MB is no floor) and RDS's `wal_keep_size` (2 GB) sits inside the `max_wal_size` window so the first timer-driven checkpoint refills too late. Control event: ten 0.2–0.28 s stalls 4–5 s apart = the ten segments the previous checkpoint had unlinked; sampler `IO:WALInitSync` + 19 in `LWLock:WALWrite`, PI 18, EM 133 MB/s at util 95 % in ~13 KB IOs while `pg_stat_io` writers were flat, pg_wal −0.67/+0.67 GB.

**Reproduced on demand** (idle 15 min → resume 12k): stock 254 ms, floor-only 196, depth-only 162, `16/16 GB` on a shallow pool 234 (the setting doesn't create segments), `16/16 GB` with the pool at depth **24.7 ms**.

**Series under the recommended setting** (`min_wal_size = max_wal_size ≥ wal_keep_size + 1.9 × peak WAL rate × checkpoint_timeout`, 16 GB): 12k b10 **5/5**, worst 10-s p99 52 ms (control 177), checkpoints all time-driven; 15k b100 **5/5**, p99 40.2–42.8 ms (stock 4/5, 43–45); 25k b100 **4/5, 0 drops, p50 36 ms** (stock 2/5 with p50 in seconds) — and the sampler shows 16 GB is one size too small at 25k (WAL 29.6 MB/s, pool hit zero twice), so the boundary is stated: 24–32 GB there.

**Honesty:** an adversarial review (3 finders, 26 findings) corrected the first draft — margin <1 segment not 10 %, `wal_keep_size` retention, T3 as a null test, stall length/share, EM `avgReqSz` in sectors, run-2 events restored to unattributed; two run-2 events remain unexplained and are named as such; a re-reading of run-2's 25k/15k as pool churn is offered as a candidate, not a finding.

**Docs:** `docs/benchmarks/sustained-throughput.md` § third run (with a first-principles explainer), `docs/ops/runbook.md` (the sizing rule, its transition cost, no `pg_switch_wal` pre-grow on RDS), rig README, CHANGELOG, MANUAL_TEST box; run-1 caveats block re-read against runs 2/3 and the failure-correctness banner de-retracted (peer audit).

**Tooling:** `provision.sh` (parameter group, PI, EM role if present, storage knobs, idempotent launch), `db-sampler.sh`, `analyze-tail.py`, `tail-census.py`, `tail-series.sh`, `provoke-walinit.sh`, `teardown.sh` inventories/deletes the parameter group.

**Product lead filed:** #823 (1.2 KB WAL / 7.7 records per event; one INSERT per event; three RI lookups with the tenants row locked 12k×/s).

## Summary

- package releases with electron-builder: signed/notarized macOS ZIP + DMG, per-user Windows NSIS, and Linux DEB/RPM

- macOS arm64/x64 Release and Nightly: automatic signed ZIP updates; DMG manual install

author: theyearistwentygx
body:
Every project has two or three commands you run constantly, and the only way to
run one from this app was to open the terminal pane and type it. That is fine
once. It is not fine when LTCDataPlus has four worktrees live, each wanting its
own dev server on its own free port.

A project declares them in `.tgxcode/commands.json`, checked in, with a
gitignored `commands.local.json` for personal overrides. The conversation header
draws a button each, acting on the session's own directory — so a worktree
session gets that worktree's dev server. A command can ask for a port range; the
app finds a free one, injects it, and names the DevBrowser tab.

```json
{ "version": 1, "commands": [{
    "id": "dev", "label": "Dev server", "run": "npm run dev",
    "port": { "range": [5000, 5099], "env": "PORT" },
    "devbrowser": "${worktree}"
}]}
```

## The decisions worth arguing about

**Config resolution is asymmetric on purpose.** A worktree is a checkout of the
same repo so it has its own `commands.json`, possibly a branch's newer one,
which should work. It never has the gitignored local file. So the shared file
comes from the directory you are running in and the personal one from the main
checkout, and your overrides follow you into every worktree. Symmetric
resolution silently loses them the moment you enter one.

**A run is a terminal with a different first command.** Not thrift — it is the
only way the output reads correctly, because vite, next and dotnet-watch all
repaint a status line with `\r` and fall back to a duller mode when they find
stdout is a pipe. `terminal.js` gained four options, each defaulting to today's
behaviour. `TerminalPool` is deliberately not reused: it keys on a session,
reaps a shell nobody is watching, and returns the existing one where a start
button must refuse.

**Runs die with their bridge, and the pane says so.** Not a limitation to route
around — the child's stdout is a pipe whose only reader is the bridge, so one
that outlived it would fill the buffer, block on `write()` and go on holding its
port while hung. Re-adoption by pid cannot help; the new bridge can acquire
neither the pipe nor the pty. Nothing is persisted as a result.

**Archiving stops runs, but only the last session out.** A dev server for a
branch nobody is looking at is exactly what holds a port for a week — but a
worktree is routinely shared, so archiving one of three must not pull the server
out from under the other two.

**Ports both bind and probe.** WSL's mirrored networking means a Windows-side
server answers on 127.0.0.1 while holding no Linux socket, so a bind test alone
hands out a port that is visibly occupied from the browser. `scripts/dev.js` now
picks its port through the same module.

## Security

This is the first time the bridge reads a file out of a project directory, or
runs a command string somebody else may have written — a `git pull` can change
what a familiar button does. The capability is not new (an API caller can
already start a session in `bypassPermissions`, or open a terminal); what is new
is that path. Treated as the same trust model as `package.json` scripts: the
resolved command is always on the button and at the head of the pane, nothing
ever auto-runs, and there is no approval flow.

What does guard it: `withinRoots` before any read or run, containment of a
command's relative `cwd`, caps of 64KB / 24 commands / 2000 chars, the env
hygiene terminals already have, `0600` on logs, and a warning when
`commands.local.json` is not actually gitignored. Reading what a project
declares is allowed remotely; running it is not — two new cases in
`test/refusals.test.js`.

Rejected as theatre: binary allowlists, arg-array-only execution, sandboxing a
process that is supposed to run indefinitely.

## Supersedes plan 13

13-A proposed re-running a command scraped out of Bash traffic; 13's own Risks
section admits that string is "long, chained, or environment-dependent". 13-B's
log keys on a port, and ports get reused across worktrees. Both are marked
superseded in place. 13's stop half stays — it works from the socket, so it is
the right tool for a server this app did not start.

## This repo declares one

`npm run dev`, on a free port in 45899–45918, DevBrowser tab named for the
worktree. The port could not travel by environment: `dev.js` reads
`CLAUDE_SESSIONS_PORT` and `terminal.js` deletes it from every run
unconditionally, so of all repos this is the one where a `port.env` block is
swallowed. `dev.js` takes `--port=` instead, behind the same refusal of 45888.

## Verified

Bridge lifecycle, port contention, DevBrowser naming against the real app,
worktree config resolution, malformed configs, the archive rule, both reapers,
and that killing a bridge orphans nothing. `npm test` passes — five suites,
including the two new refusals.

## Summary
31 of 41 tool declarations carried no `annotations=types.ToolAnnotations(...)` at all. Claude Code plan mode only auto-approves an MCP tool without a confirmation prompt when it can prove the tool is read-only via the `readOnlyHint` annotation supplied at tool-listing time — without it, every read-only lookup (`ticket_get`, `wiki_get`, `ticket_search`, ...) prompted on every call even when the caller's permission allowlist already covered it, making the server effectively unusable for read-only research in plan mode.

author: diegonava150
body:
The iOS lane has been intermittently red with `SessionNotCreatedException` wrapping a null-message `TimeoutException`. The Appium log says it plainly:

```
POST /session 200   432597 ms   <- the first session
POST /session 200    60631 ms
POST /session 200    74957 ms
POST /session 200   ~30-45 s    <- every one after
```

**432s against a 420s client ceiling.** Appium finished and returned `200` twelve seconds after the client stopped listening. Nothing was wedged — the deadline was twelve seconds too early, which is also why it failed some runs and not others.

420s was **derived, not measured**: boot ceiling + command timeout (240 + 120). That covers a boot; a cold start is more — simulator UI launch ~39s, app install ~70s, then building and launching WDA while polling `ECONNREFUSED` on 8100. Only the boot was in the sum.

Same mistake the 420s was introduced to fix, one layer out: back then the smallest timeout was the one nobody chose; here it was chosen, from the wrong quantity.

**600s** — measured 432s plus ~40%, since a shared macOS runner is exactly what will one day be slower than the one measured. A wedged session now fails in 10 min rather than 7, against a 60-min budget.

The measurement is a **unit test**, not a comment, and it refuses to be derived from the other bounds — deriving it is what went wrong. Verified by reverting to 420 and watching it fail with the measurement in the message.

**Corrects the record on the outlier:** I reported `addressFormValidatesRequiredFields` as the slow test (451s, 15.4× Android) and blamed the purchase flow. It's simply **the first test to execute**, so it absorbs the whole one-time cold start. Its own work is unremarkable, and no capability tuning would ever have touched it.

author: martinbha
body:
Closes #96.

A backup nobody has restored is a hypothesis. These commands make testing it
cheap enough to actually do, and the tests restore one and prove a transaction
written beforehand is still readable afterwards.

## What changed

- **`apps/core/backup.py`** — a sealed archive containing database rows, the
  wrapped per-user keys, the migration state, and the retained (already
  encrypted) screenshots, with a manifest recording counts and schema version.
- **Three commands** — `create_backup`, `verify_backup`, `restore_backup`.
- **`OPERATIONS.md`** — the daily/weekly/monthly schedule, the rehearsal, and the
  four-step real restore.

## Design notes

- **The master key is never in the archive.** An archive holding both is not an
  encrypted backup, it is a plaintext backup with extra steps — and the archive
  is the file most likely to reach cloud storage or a disk somebody sells. The
  manifest states its absence explicitly so a restore that cannot find a key
  knows why rather than concluding the data is corrupt, and `read_manifest`
  *refuses* an archive claiming to contain one.
- **The archive has its own passphrase**, not the master key: a backup must stay
  readable across a key rotation, and restorable by someone holding the archive
  without also holding the running system's secrets.
- **Rows are serialised, not `pg_dump`ed.** The archive is engine-independent, so
  a rehearsal restore into a disposable SQLite database is the same operation as
  a real one — which is what makes rehearsing cheap enough to happen.
- **Unpacking and loading are separate commands.** A rehearsal should inspect
  what it got before replacing anything, and the first step of a real restore is
  identical to the first step of a rehearsal.
- **The passphrase comes from the environment**, never an argument, so it stays
  out of shell history and the process list.
- **Archive entries are checked for path escape** before extraction. An archive
  is untrusted input even when it is one we wrote.

## Acceptance criteria

- **A backup can be decrypted and restored to a readable application** — the
  round trip is asserted, and a separate test deletes every transaction, reloads
  from the archive, and reads the amount and merchant back with the data key.
- **Historical transactions remain readable after restore** — 42,900 and the
  merchant both come back; a companion test asserts the serialised rows are still
  ciphertext on disk, so a backup is not where encryption quietly stops.
- **The master key is intentionally stored separately and restore steps are
  documented** — asserted three ways (raw key, encoded key, key filename all
  absent from the archive body), stated in the manifest, and written up in
  `OPERATIONS.md` with the failure it prevents.

## Verification

`uv run ruff check .`, `uv run ruff format --check .`, `uv run mypy .`, and
`uv run pytest` all pass (928 tests, 17 new).

author: skishchampi
body:
Answers the bills-date request filed today. **The endpoint serves two date formats in one record**, and the reader kept the first ten characters of whatever arrived.

| raw field | source format |
|---|---|
| `billIntroducedDate`, `billPassedInLSDate`, `billPassedInRSDate`, `referredToCommitteeDate`, `reportPresentedDate` | `YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.0` |
| **`billAssentedDate`** | **`DD/MM/YYYY`** |

So `assent_date: "20/12/2025"` sat beside `passed_ls_date: "2025-12-16"` under a field name that implies ISO.

**What it produced.** A two-year count of bills that became law compared those strings against ISO bounds and reported **0**. The true figure is **53**. Nothing raised, no field was empty, the run looked clean. An independent `actYear` count in the same record caught it — a period holding 59 Acts cannot hold zero assents.

## ⚠ Re-run the bills probe

Rows already on disk carry the raw value. No figure computed from `assent_date` can be trusted until they are re-fetched.

## What changed

- Every date field is parsed and emitted as ISO. Four formats are known and named in one constant.
- A value matching none of them raises `UnreadableDate`, naming the value and the formats tried, rather than entering the record truncated.
- **One unreadable date no longer discards a whole house.** The crawl caught exceptions per house, so a single bad record would abort the walk and leave one `fetch_error` where thousands of good records belonged. A bad record is now `parse_error` and the walk continues — this package's own invariant.
- The schema's `fetch_status` enum grew to match, and a real `parse_error` record was validated against it rather than assumed to fit. No pattern is pinned on `assent_date`, because that would reject the rows already on disk.

## Verification

- **Live against the endpoint:** 200 records on page 1, 42 carrying an assent date, `06/08/2026` normalising to `2026-08-06`, zero values this reader cannot read.
- 1732 passed, ruff clean. Ten tests, each failing first.

## Not established

Whether any other sansad endpoint mixes date formats. Only the bills endpoint was tested, here and by the filer.

author: nickysemenza
body:
The **Add to Inventory** dialog on a product page asked for a location and offered no help finding one, in a house with a few hundred of them. Every other classification field in the app has a Sparkles **Suggest** button; the field that actually needs one didn't.

It also seeded the amount unit empty while `amount` requires `unit: z.string().min(1)`, so the first submit of every add bounced off validation. Effectively every live entry in the ledger uses the same unit, so the empty default bought nothing.

## Why a model and not a ranking

I backtested a deterministic ranker (same-tag + same-manufacturer + same-category sibling counts, weighted 5/3/1) against every existing inventory entry: **top-1 22%, top-3 37%**. Counts are weak here because the largest category alone spreads across dozens of locations with the leader holding 8%.

What counts can't see is that a tool-system accessory belongs on the wall its family already occupies — that's a read of the location's **name**. So the sibling counts go into the prompt as corroboration and the model does the choosing.

## What changed

**Server**

- `getLocationPutAwayCandidates` (`repo/location/lookup.ts`) — every live location with its ancestor chain, item count, and same-tag / same-manufacturer / same-category counts for the source product. Modeled on `getTagSiblingStorage`: same joins, same `notDeleted` + `stockOnly()` guards, same "the source raises `holdsProduct` but is never its own sibling" rule. Aggregated per location in SQL rather than folded over raw entries, so the interactive call stays one small grouped scan as the ledger grows. Unstocked locations are included — an empty shelf is a fine destination.
- `services/ai-enrichment/location-suggest.ts` — assembles the prompt, calls Haiku, and **matches the returned code back against the roster** before it reaches the client. The model-facing output schema uses a plain `z.string()` for the id; the branded `locationShortcode` only appears on the tRPC output, after validation. A code that names no candidate throws `AI_SUGGESTION_UNUSABLE` (a new 5xx reason — a suggester ignoring its own roster is a prompt/provider regression worth seeing in Sentry, not a normal empty result).
- `ai.suggestLocation` — a `.query()`, like the other two pure suggesters. Runs inline, per the tenet that rare interactive work stays off the background queue.

**Client**

- `LocationFieldWithAI` — `FieldWithAISuggest` takes its field as a node, so the existing location combobox goes in untouched. No new suggestion pattern, and none of the hand-rolled duplication `with-usda-food-search.tsx` fell into.
- Registered in the dev AI smoke test so it isn't invisible to the sweep.

**The default unit**

- One exported `DEFAULT_AMOUNT_UNIT`, used by `quick-inventory-add` (4 sites) and `inventory-form`. The four sites in `SessionCaptureActions` that already hardcoded the same literal now point at it too.

## Verification

`pnpm check` exits 0 (biome, typecheck, knip, both convention guards). 2,252 unit+ui and 1,114 integration tests pass.

New coverage:

| Tier | Pins |
| --- | --- |
| integration (6) | Sibling counts exclude the source; `holdsProduct` flips only for the source's own rows; an installed fixture is not somewhere to put a spare; an emptied (soft-deleted) entry stops counting; the placeholder manufacturer and a null category are not shared identities. |
| unit (7) | Line formatting incl. the ancestor chain and zero-hint omission; the roster cap discloses its omission; a known code resolves to the candidate's own shortcode and name; an invented code throws; a truncated code is not prefix-matched. |
| ui (3) | The suggestion writes into the field and renders its reasoning; a failure leaves the field alone; the form submits a complete amount without the operator typing a unit. |

I checked that the unit test genuinely fails when the default is reverted, rather than passing vacuously.

Driven in the browser against real data on two products the count heuristic would have missed — a tool-system accessory and a spice — both landed on the obviously correct location with `high` confidence. Metered as expected: `location-suggestion` / `suggestLocation`, ~7.2k in / ~80 out, **$0.008**, ~5s.

## Reviewer notes

- **No inventory row was actually saved during verification.** The dev server points at the production database, so completing an add would have written a real row, and removing it would be a soft delete — permanent here. The submit path is untouched by this change.
- **A pre-existing hydration error** appears in the dev console on product pages. I confirmed it fires on the stashed baseline too, so it is not from this change; worth its own fix.
- The Suggest button is wired only into this dialog. `LocationFieldWithAI` is reusable if we want it on the other location pickers.
