author: arvavit
body:
Stacked on #1055.

Production right now: two **published** Daily Challenge questions whose answer options have no German and no Ukrainian row at all. A German opening the card on those days gets a legible question and four blank buttons — the exact failure this module was written to end, still happening.

Nothing failed. Nothing was ever attempted. The sweep that selects work looked for rows sitting at `failed`, and for machine rows whose `source_hash` was cleared. A row that does not exist is neither, so the question looked settled and was skipped — every night, indefinitely.

Same lesson as #1037, when the selector counted only `question_text` and 57 explanations were invisible: **if the selection is the only pass, it has to be complete.** "Failed" and "never existed" are different states, and only one of them was being looked for.

The selector now reads every field of the question and of every option and asks whether there is a servable row in each language. A locale parked at `needs_review` still does not count as work — at temperature 0 re-asking returns the same verdict, and counting it would spend every night's budget on the two questions a person has to look at anyway. `/retry-reviewed` parks rows at `failed`, which has no servable row, so re-opened work comes straight back here.

## Verification

The new test deletes the German option rows from a fully-translated question and asserts the sweep picks it up again. Under the old selector it did not: nothing was `failed`, so nothing was outstanding.

2389 backend tests green.

## Production follow-up

Once deployed, the nightly sweep repairs the five rows itself (limit 2 questions per night). Worth watching rather than assuming.

author: tiyfiy
body:
Closes MY-19.

Turns the light Flighty-style direction into tokens. Every later UI issue reads
colour, type and spacing from here.

## What landed

```
Pacer/DesignSystem/
├── Colors.swift              semantic roles, backed by the asset catalogue
├── Typography.swift          type scale + tracking
├── Spacing.swift             8pt grid, radii, layout constants, card shadow
├── SessionType+Style.swift   zone tint, pill colours, labels, purpose lines
└── DesignSystemPreview.swift the reference sheet, light and dark
```

Plus 21 colour sets (light + dark variants each), `SessionType` in `TrainingKit`,
and `PacerTests/DesignSystemTests.swift`.

## Contrast is measured, not eyeballed

`DesignSystemTests` re-derives the WCAG ratio for every text token against every
surface it can sit on, in both schemes, straight from the shipped asset
catalogue. It also renders `"111"` and `"888"` and asserts equal widths — the
direct test that a column of paces lines up.

| token | light | dark | target |
|---|---|---|---|
| textPrimary | 15.3:1 | 17.0:1 | AAA |
| textSecondary | 4.6:1 | 4.6:1 | AA |
| textTertiary | 3.1:1 | 3.0:1 | AA large |
| positive | 4.6:1 | 5.6:1 | AA |
| negative | 5.9:1 | 4.5:1 | AA |
| zone pill labels | ≥4.5:1 | ≥4.5:1 | AA on their own pill |

The six zone colours are the spec values verbatim in both schemes. Only the pill
*label* colour is derived — the raw tint is picked to work as a fill and does not
clear AA as text on its own 12% wash.

## Three things to decide

The direction is silent on these, so I picked something defensible rather than
blocking, but they are yours to overrule:

1. **White on accent measures 4.20:1** — just under AA. A 17pt/600 button label
   on `#EC3013` is not accessible. Either the accent darkens to about `#D42B11`,
   or button labels go to ≥18.5pt semibold to qualify as large text. I left the
   accent at the spec value and documented the gap.
2. **Secondary/tertiary text alphas were raised** (0.60→0.73, 0.45→0.57). The
   spec values are Apple's own `secondaryLabel`, which measures 3.05:1 and fails
   AA for body copy. The AC asked for AA, so contrast won over fidelity.
3. **`negative` was invented** — the direction has no "missed/warning" colour, and
   the accent red is spoken for. I used `#B3261E`, deep enough to read as
   distinct from the accent.

Two smaller deviations, both documented in the source:

- `Font.body` / `Font.caption` are named **`bodyText` / `captionText`**. SwiftUI
  owns those two names; redeclaring them does not shadow cleanly — inside this
  module ours quietly wins, and from any other module the reference is ambiguous
  and fails to compile (it did, in the test target).
- Colour sets are prefixed `Palette…` because Xcode generates a `Color` member per
  asset name, which collided with every token (and `Separator` collided with
  UIKit's own). The catalogue holds raw palette entries; `Colors.swift` names the
  roles; screens only ever see the roles.

## SessionType

The ticket's `SessionType+Style.swift` needs a `SessionType` to extend, and there
wasn't one. Added to `TrainingKit` as the enum and its Z1–Z6 intensity ramp only —
raw values pinned by a test since they will be persisted. MY-28 still owns the
workout step model.

Note also that MY-18's `/design/DIRECTION.md` is not in the repo; I worked from
the direction section embedded in the MY-19 description, which carries all the
values.

## Verification

- `xcodebuild test` — 12 design system tests, all UI tests, zero warnings
- `swift test --package-path TrainingKit` — 4 tests
- Preview sheet rendered and inspected in both schemes

author: pablof7z-agent
body:
Closes #1888. Reproduces and documents #1889. Advances #1887 to a definite, negative answer.

Two Canary scenarios against a real strfry child process, through the public `NMP` facade only. **One is green and one is red, and the red one is the more valuable result.**

## C14 — NIP-77 negentropy reconciliation. Proven.

`C14Nip77ReconciliationTests.swift` holds one feed open across a real relay outage during which the relay's LMDB store gains ten events the local Redb store does not have. The divergence is written by a second strfry process over the same `dataDir` on its own ephemeral port while the app's port provably refuses a TCP connection — C13's mechanism, so it is deterministic rather than a race won.

**The oracle is not "the events arrived."** That is equally true of a plain REQ that resends all 70. It is `RelayDiagnostics.eventsByKind` — "events actually RECEIVED from a relay" — sampled before the outage and again after convergence:

| relay config | converged | events transferred across the reconnect | `nip77Handoff` history |
|---|---|---|---|
| `negentropy.enabled = true` | 70/70 | **10** (60 → 70) | `none → awaiting_live_eose → backfilling → live` |
| `negentropy.enabled = false` | 70/70 | **70** (60 → 130) | `none` |

Both runs are committed as separate tests. Neither half is evidence alone: "converged" without the count says nothing about NIP-77, and the count without the negentropy-off control is not evidence the count is *caused* by NIP-77.

**Falsified three ways**, each restored and re-confirmed green:
1. Seeding the divergence *before* the outage instead of during it left convergence trivially true and was caught only by the divergence precondition (`the app already held 10 outage-window events before the outage ended`). C13's fourth falsifier, same shape.
2. Inverting the efficiency assertion failed on the real captured `10` against a deliberately wrong `60`.
3. Pointing the negentropy scenario at the negentropy-disabled relay failed all four NIP-77 assertions at once with real values: `advertised_unsupported`, `unknown`, handoff `["none"]`, 70 events.

### Two findings from writing it

- **A cold start never reconciles; it always refetches.** The first draft primed the store, shut the engine down, seeded the divergence and restarted — the obvious shape. It converged *while receiving all 70 events*, with NMP simultaneously reporting `nip77Behavior = behaviorally_proven` and `nip77Handoff = none`. `begin_neg_handoff` is only reachable when the prober already holds a verdict at the moment a request is placed; the probe is asynchronous, a fresh engine sends its REQ as soon as the socket is up, and nothing re-plans the in-flight request. Reconciliation engages on the *next* request. The committed scenario therefore establishes the probe verdict first and asserts it as a precondition.
- **Reconciliation is invisible per query.** NIP-77 coverage is attributed through the same `attribute_eose` path as an ordinary EOSE, so `SourceEvidence.reconciledThrough` and `SourceStatus` are identical either way. The only public distinguisher is the engine-global, per-relay `nip77Advertisement`/`nip77Behavior`/`nip77Handoff` triple — and `nip77Handoff` is a transient an app must accumulate from `observeDiagnostics()` to see at all.

## C15 — NIP-42 AUTH. Red on purpose: the NMP path does not work.

`canary.md` recorded C15's relay lab as qualified and C15 itself as not proven, because the only live round trip on record was driven by the test *controller*. This PR drives `NMPEngine` — and it deadlocks.

**Every precondition passes**, each proven by a new NMP-free `RelayLabKit.probeRead`:

- an unauthenticated plain client issuing the identical filter receives a real `["AUTH", <challenge>]` plus `CLOSED ... auth-required: requested filter requires authentication`, and zero events;
- a client that authenticates as a **different** key completes the handshake (`successfully authenticated`) and is still served zero events (`restrictReadToInvolvedPubkey` is left on, and the seeded events are `p`-tagged to NMP's own account, so "the row arrived" would have meant "NMP authenticated *as its own account*");
- a client that authenticates as an involved pubkey is served the row.

**Then NMP transmits nothing at all.** Not the AUTH proof — not even the REQ. It opens the `.nip42` session, reports it under exactly the requested access identity, reaches `awaitingAuth(phase: .awaitingChallenge)` and stays there. The installed `NMPAuthPolicy` is never consulted; `AuthDiagnostics` reports `policyBound=false`, `signerBound=false`, `challengeDescriptor=nil`.

**A control phase pins the cause through the public API alone** — same relay, same filter, one field different:

```
CONTROL (.public):  status=error                           history=["connecting", "error"]
SUBJECT (.nip42):   status=awaitingAuth(awaitingChallenge)  history=["connecting", "awaitingAuth(awaitingChallenge)"]
```

The public session's REQ reaches the relay and is answered (with the auth-required refusal, hence `error`). The protected session is the one that never transmits. Recorded, not asserted — a diagnosis printed alongside a failure, the same treatment C13 gave `wireSubCount`.

The mechanism (#1889): NMP drops a protected session's ops from the wire delta until AUTH completes, replays planned REQs at connect only for a `Public` session, and constructs an `AuthSessionState` only on an **inbound** `["AUTH", challenge]` frame. strfry only challenges **in response to** a request it wants to gate. Neither side is wrong alone; together they never exchange a byte.

**Why nothing caught it before:** every green NIP-42 test either injects a synthetic challenge straight into the reducer, or uses a relay hand-built to challenge unsolicited on connect — `integration_capstone.rs`'s bespoke relay says so in its own comment, and it exists precisely because the standard fixture does not. The only relay shape the current engine can complete a round trip against is one built for it.

**Left red rather than reshaped**, on the principle C17's #1846 phase established. The round trip, the denial surfacing as `authDenied`, recovery on a fresh session, and re-AUTH after a reconnect are all already asserted with their preconditions, so closing #1889 is what turns it green.

**Falsified twice**, each restored and the red state re-confirmed. Since the *result* is a failure, the *preconditions* are what had to be falsifiable: pointing `restrictedReadKinds` at an unused kind made the unauthenticated probe be served the row outright (three preconditions red, and the `.public` control turned green, confirming the auth gate is the only thing holding it at `error`); turning `restrictReadToInvolvedPubkey` off made the wrong-identity probe be served the row, failing exactly that one precondition and nothing else.

## Also in this PR

- `RelayLabKit/RestrictedReadProbe.swift` — one plain NMP-free `REQ` on one fresh connection reporting what the relay did about it, optionally completing a NIP-42 handshake as a caller-supplied key first. It exists so a scenario can prove a relay's demand *independently of NMP*: "NMP got the row, therefore the relay demanded AUTH" is circular.
- `docs/internals/canary.md` — C14 and C15 scenario status rewritten, including the plain statement that C15's NMP path does not work, and the stale lead-in to the old controller-driven qualification corrected.
- `docs/known-gaps.md` — three new entries (#1889, and C14's two findings).
- `apps/Canary/CanaryScenarios/README.md` — names the two scenarios that are red on purpose, so a full `swift test` not being all-green is not read as a broken checkout.

## Verification

`swift test` from `apps/Canary/CanaryScenarios`, full suite:

```
C1  passed   C2  passed   C7  passed   C9  passed (3/3)   C13 passed
C14 passed (2/2)
C15 failed  (2/2 — #1889, the result)
C17 passed (2/3), distinct phase failed (#1846, pre-existing)
```

Not merged. No production code touched

author: hbmartin
body: ## Summary - rank tied Beauty finalists by an explicit topological-buildability tier, then grounding and symmetry, so floating clusters cannot beat grounded layouts and flat mosaics retain aesthetics-first selection - treat one-ULP-equivalent axis costs as ties, share deadlines through one clamped helper, and skip expensive topology/symmetry work for a single finalist - add cached `TopologyMetrics` so component count, component labels, and floating IDs share one sparse labeling across placement, analysis, pipeline, redesign, bundle, and SNOT consumers - reuse finalization telemetry metrics during finalist selection instead of rebuilding an unchanged connection graph - make CI Python-version verification accept both minor and patch pins, and harden deadline/renderer regression helpers - update placement and representation documentation for the new behavior ## Why The previous lexicographic key ranked raw brick-graph component count before grounding. That could select a single entirely floating cluster over grounded free-standing towers, and on ground-level mosaics component count collapsed to brick count and silently outranked symmetry. Exact float equality could also prevent mathematically tied axis runs from reaching post-finalization selection. ## Impact Beauty placement now preserves feasibility and grounding guarantees without sacrificing the aesthetics preset on flat models. Repeated topology queries and telemetry-enabled finalist selection avoid redundant graph construction and connected-components work. ## Validation - `uv run ruff format --check .` - `uv run ruff check .` - `uv run ty check src tests` - `uv run pyrefly check src tests` - `uv run pytest` — 1,458 passed, 9 skipped - `git diff --check` ## Summary by CodeRabbit - **New Features** - Added unified topology metrics for component counts, floating elements, grounding, and buildability. - Added filled-component counting for voxel grids. - Added deadline-sharing support for time-limited operations. - **Improvements** - Layered placement now handles near-equal candidates more reliably, prioritizing buildable and grounded results. - Reused cached topology calculations for more consistent and efficient analysis. - **Bug Fixes** - Improved deadline handling when time has expired. - Updated rendering and placement checks for more robust behavior. - **Documentation** - Clarified topology metrics, deadline handling, and placement tie-breaking behavior. --- ## Summary by cubic Fixes Beauty finalist selection to prefer buildable and grounded results, and reuses cached topology metrics to avoid rebuilding connection graphs. Previously, finalists ranked raw component count before grounding and required exact float equality; now selection tiers by feasibility, treats 1e-12 cost deltas as ties, and splits remaining deadlines deterministically. - Finalist ranking: select a buildable result first (no floating bricks and component count ≤ grid filled-component floor), then grounded over floating. Within a tier, sort by symmetry error, then floating count, component excess, and brick count. Flat mosaics keep symmetry-first selection. - Tiling ties: treat costs equal within 1e-12 as ties; share remaining time with `deadline_share`; skip selection work for a single finalist. - Topology reuse: introduce `TopologyMetrics` (component_count, floating_ids, labels) and cache it on `ConnectionGraph`. Methods delegate to this cache; ground reachability derives from brick-only labels. - Runtime and grid: add `deadline_share` and `VoxelGrid.filled_component_count` for accurate feasibility floors and consistent time slicing. - Pipeline, analysis, SNOT, redesign, orchestrator, and greedy placement now call `topology_metrics()` and avoid duplicate labeling. - CI/tests: keep all matrix jobs running; Python version check accepts minor or minor.patch; tests no longer rely on corpus files and harden renderer command discovery. Written for commit 270b346511ec9025d99a5fbfb7d018c46f338921. Summary will update on new commits.

author: randyzwitch
body:
## What

A native TrueType (`sfnt`/`glyf`) font file parser -- `canvas_mojo/text/ttf.mojo` -- reading a font file's own binary tables directly rather than linking FreeType. This is the "why not" experiment we discussed: of this package's two remaining FFI dependencies, FreeType (closed, stable binary format) is the tractable one to replace natively; fontconfig (open-ended, continuously-updated OS convention) stays linked, for the reasons `font_discovery.mojo`'s own docstring already gives.

## Scope (v1, matching `io/png.mojo`'s own established pattern)

- **TrueType (`glyf`) outlines only** -- a CFF/OpenType-CFF font raises a clear error rather than being silently misread.
- **No hinting** -- skipped on purpose; every glyph goes through `fill_path_aa`'s own supersampled AA anyway, which makes unhinted outlines look correct at chart-relevant sizes (verified directly, see below).
- **Variable fonts** read their default instance automatically, by simply never touching `gvar`'s own per-instance deltas.
- **Composite glyphs** (accented characters, e.g. "é") are supported, including the scale/2x2-transform component flags; point-matching placement mode is not, and raises a clear error if hit.

## Methodology

Every field offset and decode algorithm was transcribed directly from Microsoft's OpenType 1.9.1 specification (not guessed at or reconstructed from memory) -- same discipline already used for FreeType's own `FT_Outline_Decompose` and zlib's own `puff.c`.

## Verification

- Parsing DejaVu Sans gives `unitsPerEm=2048`, `numGlyphs=6253`, `ascender=1901`, `descender=-483` -- the **exact same values** already independently verified against FreeType itself elsewhere in this codebase.
- A from-scratch Python oracle (plain `struct.unpack`, no font libraries, written independently while developing this) cross-checked every stage before being trusted: table offsets, both `cmap` subtable formats (4 and 12 independently agree on the same glyph indices for the same codepoints), the simple-glyph decode ("I" -- 1 contour, 4 points, all on-curve, matching the FreeType path's own already-locked-in fact), and the composite-glyph transform math (the full 32-point, 3-contour decomposition of "é" diffed byte-for-byte against the oracle before being locked into a test).
- Closed the loop end to end: the natively-parsed "O" glyph, rendered through `fill_path_aa`, produces real ink with a correctly `EVEN_ODD`-punched hole. Compared directly against the same test through the existing FreeType path: close but not pixel-identical (391 vs. 374 ink pixels, 31.48px vs 31.0px advance) -- a real, understood, expected gap: FreeType applies its own default hinting/rounding even without an explicit "no hinting" flag; this module deliberately never does. Confirmed the underlying *raw* outline data matches the oracle exactly first, so this is FreeType's own post-processing, not a parsing discrepancy.

## Status

Ships as a standalone, thoroughly-tested module (9 tests, `tests/test_ttf.mojo`) -- **not yet wired into `draw_text`/`measure_text`**, matching the exact incremental pattern `font_discovery.mojo` shipped in on its own during the original Cairo removal, before later modules wired it in. Swapping this in as `glyph_outline.mojo`'s actual outline source (replacing FreeType there too) is the natural next step, not done in this same change.

Full suite: 249 tests (240 existing + 9 new), zero regressions.

body:
The single test in the suite that changes outcome as the clock advances — the whole yield of #200's sweep.

## Measured, not reasoned

Shifting today (with **both** the `src` and test `date` bindings patched, so the comparison moves together):

```
2027-03-31  green
2027-04-01  RED     <- Q1 2027 completed; "2027Q1 is not complete" became false
```

Before:

```python
def test_is_quarter_complete_future():
    # Q1 2027 ends March 31, 2027; today is May 5, 2026     <- already stale
    assert is_quarter_complete("2027Q1") is False
```

The comment was wrong when I found it (today was 2026-08-17), which is the same defect one level down.

## After

Derives the quarter **after** the one containing today. Verified green at +0 / +227 / +400 / +1000 / +4000 days — through 2037 — and across the Q4 → next-year-Q1 rollover at 2026-12-01, 12-15 and 12-31.

Deliberately the **next** quarter rather than the current one: on the last day of a quarter the current quarter completes, so anchoring there would flake four days a year.

## The rule it is an instance of

In the docstring, because it generalises past this test: **an assertion that something HAS happened is stable; an assertion that something has NOT YET happened expires.** Its siblings — "2025Q4 is complete", "2026Q1 is complete" — never needed touching, for exactly that reason. Any "not yet" claim carries a date whether it says so or not.

## Scope

One test, one file, rewritten in place. Suite **13 failed / 1708 passed / 27 skipped**, unchanged from the baseline at b277a85 — no count change, and the 13 are the same #177 + #187's twelve.

## Context from the sweep

#200 was filed on the premise that more date-sensitive ambient tests were lurking. Measured: **241 tests across 49 files** open a real DB or the real uploads dir, and **zero** change outcome when the price cache advances by up to 30 days. Exactly one changes outcome when the clock advances — this one — and it is not an ambient DB read at all. The three originally-cited instances were all already fixed, including `test_asof_inception_line.py`'s two, which pin `frontier=_TODAY` explicitly with the reason in their docstring.

Guards up throughout, down only for the suite run; `demo.db` restored to HEAD by per-table fingerprint (302 price + 3 dividend rows of cache drift). No data file in this commit.

author: mmatheson
body:
## Why

The file we report for an XCTest / swift-testing case comes from the failure summary, and for a failure *raised inside a helper* that is the helper's file — a snapshot trait, a mocking framework, a page object, a launch helper. Those live under the package checkout, so we report e.g.:

```
/Users/anka/builds/zillow/ios/apps/ZillowMap/Tuist/.build/checkouts/ZUITesting/Sources/ZUITesting/PageObject.swift
/Users/anka/builds/zillow/ios/apps/ZillowMap/Tuist/.build/checkouts/swift-snapshot-testing/Sources/SnapshotTesting/SnapshotsTestTrait.swift
```

Codeowners are resolved from that path (`context/src/junit/parser.rs`), so the test then belongs to whoever owns the vendored directory. For ZillowGroup that is `Tuist/ @reviewers/mobile-app-platform-ios`, and it is a recurring support thread — 683 of their currently-active test cases sit on such a path, 940 rows owned by that team as a result.

## The mechanism

From our own fixture's `database.sqlite3` (`SourceCodeFrames.orderInContainer`, innermost first):

| order | symbolName | filePath |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 | `recordIssue(_:fileID:filePath:line:column:)` | `…/SourcePackages/checkouts/swift-snapshot-testing` |
| 4 | `assertSnapshot<A, B>(of:as:…)` | `…/SourcePackages/checkouts/swift-snapshot-testing` |
| **5** | **`SnapshotReproTests.failingSnapshot()`** | **`…/Tests/SnapshotReproTests/SnapshotReproTests.swift`** |
| 12 | `closure #1 in _SnapshotsTestTrait.provideScope(…)` | `…/checkouts/swift-snapshot-testing` |

The test's own frame is in the **middle** — helpers it called below it, the framework that invoked it above — so `find_file_in_source_code_context_call_stack`'s `.last()` selects a dependency by construction. It returns the right answer on this fixture only incidentally: those dependency locations point at the package *directory*, so the `.swift`/`.m` extension filter drops them. Zillow's dependency frames are real `.swift` files, so nothing stops them.

## What changed

**1. Select the frame whose symbol names the test.** Matched for Swift (`Suite.testCase()`), Objective-C (`-[Suite testCase]`), closures declared inside the test (`closure #1 in …`, still the test's file), and top-level swift-testing functions, which have no suite — a shape Zillow raised separately. That frame's file is a positive identification rather than a blocklist of everything else.

`imageName` looks like the natural discriminator and **is not**: SPM dependencies are statically linked into the test bundle, so every frame in the fixture — including the ones inside swift-snapshot-testing — reports `imageName = SnapshotReproTests`. Worth recording so nobody reaches for it later.

**2. Reject vendored dependency paths from the remaining sources** — the raised-from `fileName`, the source-code-context location, the last-frame fallback, and the document location used by the non-experimental path (otherwise the fix leaks straight through it). Segments: `/.build/`, `/checkouts/`, `/DerivedData/`, which covers both the Tuist layout and stock SPM under DerivedData.

When a test crashes or fails to launch it never reaches its own frame and every remaining source points into a dependency — we now report **no file** rather than one that would re-own the test. Consumers treat a missing file as "unchanged", not "cleared" (the ETL only takes non-empty values), so the test keeps the path and owners it last had.

## Behaviour change worth a reviewer's judgement

This also changes attribution for a failure raised inside an **in-repo** helper: the test's own file now wins over the helper's. That is the intended reading of "the file of the test case", and it is what makes ownership follow the test rather than the utility it called — but it is broader than the dependency case in the title, so flagging it explicitly.

## Tests

`cargo test -p xcresult --lib` — 24 pass, including new cases for: the test frame outranking a raised-from path; ObjC and closure symbols; a dependency `fileName` falling through to the location; dependency frames skipped in the last-frame fallback; a dependency-only summary (the crash/launch case) yielding `None`; a dependency document location rejected in the fallback map; and suite-less swift-testing functions.

`cargo fmt` clean; `cargo clippy -p xcresult` surfaces nothing new (the two warnings on this file, `Iterator::last` and an elidable lifetime, are pre-existing).

**Not run:** the `#[cfg(target_os = "macos")]` integration tests, which need `xcresulttool` — I only have Linux here. `test_swift_snapshot_testing_trait_failure_uses_assertion_file` should still pass unchanged (its expected file is the test file, which is exactly what the symbol-matched frame yields), but please confirm on a Mac before merge.

**Also worth adding before this ships:** a fixture built from one of the xcresults Zillow shared in #trunk-zillow — specifically a UI-test launch failure and a `PageObject` timeout, since those are the shapes I could only reconstruct synthetically here.

## Related

trunk2 #5254 fixes the read side — the ClickHouse views that were showing a test's creation-time path forever and blanking collection-scoped codeowners on any upload that reported no file. This PR stops the bad path being written; that one stops a corrected path being ignored.

author: robmry
body:
## Description

The Sandboxes credential pages describe the keychain-less Linux fallback as "an encrypted file" and quote a CLI notice that no longer exists. They also frame the fallback as weaker than an OS keychain only because a keychain "mediates access per application".

Both understate it. The file is encrypted with a key compiled into `sbx`, not a secret the user holds, so anyone who can read the file can decrypt it. What actually protects it is the `0700` directory mode — which the pages already mention, so this mostly moves the emphasis onto the claim that holds.

`sbx` now prints:

```text
No keychain detected - this secret will be stored on disk, protected by file permissions rather than a password
```

replacing the previous "…stored in an encrypted file on disk". The quoted strings here are byte-matched against the constant in the CLI.

Four passages change:

- `security/credentials.md` — the fallback description, the quoted notice, and the protection claim
- `security/credentials.md` — the **Best practices** list, which repeated "encrypted at rest in the OS keychain (or an encrypted file on Linux hosts without a keychain)"
- `faq.md` — the headless-Linux entry, which carried the same notice and claim

No behaviour or feature is being documented here — only the accuracy of an existing description.

## Related issues or tickets

The CLI-side change is in `docker/sandboxes` and ships in the next release. Worth holding this until that release is out: until then the page would quote a notice users don't see yet.

## Reviews

- [ ] Technical review
- [ ] Editorial review
- [ ] Product review

Two things a reviewer may want to weigh in on:

- **Tone.** The intent is to be accurate without being alarming: it states what protects the file and what the encryption does and does not give you, rather than editorialising about weakness. Happy to soften or sharpen.
- **Adjacent advice, unchanged here.** The FAQ paragraph immediately below the edited text tells headless users to install `gnome-keyring` and start `dbus-run-session`. A *locked* Secret Service collection is known to make `sbx` commands hang rather than fall back, and on a key-only SSH host locked is the default state after the keyring daemon restarts — so that advice can land users somewhere worse than the fallback. It is left alone because the underlying issue is being worked separately, but it may deserve a caveat once that is resolved.

<sub>Investigated, authored and posted by Claude Code on behalf of @robmry.</sub>

author: ajbarea
body:
`make ci` says it runs every CI gate "exactly as the workflow does". It skipped two of
them, and the test that exists to catch exactly that could not see either.

## The two steps

| step in `ci.yml` | in `make ci` |
| --- | --- |
| `uv run python -c "from pharos import telemetry; assert telemetry.configure() is False"` | missing |
| `uv run pip-audit` | missing |

Both now run locally, in the positions they hold remotely: the telemetry assertion ahead
of the lint trio, `pip-audit` after the suite so a CVE in a transitive dependency cannot
mask a real test failure. `pip-audit` is the only step in the target that reaches the
network, which is noted beside it.

Found by running the workflow's steps by hand against a tree where `make ci` had just
passed green.

## Why the existing check missed them

`_workflow_runs()` collected lines beginning `run:`. That is only true of a step written
with a `name:`, because a bare step begins `- run:` and the dash comes first. Every
measurement step in `ci.yml` is named, so the existing comparison worked and looked
complete --- while the lint trio, the folded `pytest` invocation, the telemetry assertion
and `pip-audit` were all invisible to it.

It parses the YAML now, which also makes the multi-line gate loop legible for the first
time.

## The new assertion

`test_make_ci_runs_the_workflows_tool_steps_too` compares everything that is not a
measurement script, in the same excused-with-a-reason shape the exclusions in this file
already use:

- `uv sync --all-groups` is named in `WORKFLOW_ONLY`: setup the target assumes, not a gate
  it skips.
- Codecov-only flags (`--cov-report=xml`, `--junitxml`, `-o junit_family=legacy`) are
  dropped before matching, since no local step uploads anything.
- Commands are normalized for whitespace, `$$`, quotes and `;`, so a loop written across
  three lines in YAML and one line in make compares equal.

## Verification

Tripped by deleting each of `pip-audit`, the telemetry assertion, `ty check`, `ruff check`
and the `pytest` line from the `ci` target in turn --- every one turns it red, and the
unmodified tree is green. `make lint` clean.

A first pass at this reported the gate loop as missing, which was the normalizer rather
than the target: the workflow separates loop clauses with newlines where the one-liner
needs a semicolon. That is typography, and it is normalized away rather than excused.

author: jegr78
body:
Part of the roster synchronisation work for #74. **Third of five stacked pull requests**, targeting the second. Merge in order.

## What this adds

A club uploads its export and sees exactly what it would change. Nothing is written: every creation, every field of every update, every membership that would end, every row that could not be read, and every creation that resembles somebody the roster already holds.

The distinction that matters is **header versus cell**. A header problem fails the whole file, because nothing in it can then be trusted. A cell problem fails one row and is reported beside the rest — a club with one truncated line should not have to repair its export before it can see the other nine hundred rows.

A preview is immutable and supersedes its predecessor rather than replacing it. Correcting a mistake means uploading the corrected file: an editable preview would no longer be what anybody reviewed, and reviewing is its entire purpose. The SHA-256 of the uploaded bytes is reported so a board can tell it reviewed the file it meant to.

## The test that was asserting nothing

Ownership is what keeps a club's own corrections: a field the source does not own is never written, however different the file is. That branch is the one this change could get quietly wrong, so it was mutation-tested.

**Flipping the ownership check to always-true left the suite green.** The fixture happened to give the file and the roster the same address, so the unowned field never differed and the test exercised nothing. With a file that genuinely disagrees, the mutant dies — as does one that ignores `FULL_SNAPSHOT` versus `UPDATE_ONLY`.

Worth knowing about when reading the resolver tests: the fixtures are load-bearing.

## Two decisions worth reviewing

**A column the mapping does not name is listed, not fatal.** The plan said such a header should be "reported rather than ignored", and refusing the file outright would make real imports impossible — a club's export carries bank details and addresses this product deliberately does not want. Listing them keeps both halves: nothing is dropped silently, and data minimisation survives. A column left out by a typo in the mapping looks exactly like a column the club never wanted, and only the club can tell them apart.

**The removal threshold's denominator is the source's own current memberships**, not the whole roster. A source covering part of a club would otherwise never reach any threshold — which is exactly the case where a truncated export does the most damage unnoticed.

## A guard that was proving nothing

`AdminSurfaceTest` assumed every admin endpoint consumes JSON, so the first multipart endpoint made its routing probe report a misroute. It now takes each endpoint's own consumable media type from the mapping. The guard was right to fail: it was proving nothing about that endpoint.

## From the whole-stack self-review

Two things were fixed here after reviewing the finished stack:

**`import_preview.raw_content` is gone.** It held the complete uploaded CSV and nothing in `src/main` ever read it — the change set in the same row already carries the same names, addresses and member numbers and is what an execution needs. The column stored a second copy of a club's membership list for no purpose.

**Finding a possible duplicate read the entire `person` table on every upload** to answer a question about the names in one file. It now looks up only the names the file carries.

## Operations

An oversized upload is answered `413` with a problem document rather than a container error page. Two new settings — `COURTSIDE_IMPORT_MAX_FILE_SIZE` and `COURTSIDE_IMPORT_PREVIEW_RETENTION` — are documented in `deploy/README.md` with every other environment variable.

## Verification

`./mvnw clean verify` green.

author: tctai141-collab
body:
Remediates both audits — the first technical audit and the independent verification pass that found the first one missed the most serious issues. Where they disagree, the verification report wins.

**Do not issue the 20 founder invite links until C-1…C-4 below are confirmed closed and the human follow-up at the bottom is done.**

```
install    PASS   lockfile in sync
typecheck  PASS   0 errors (was 27) — now also covers scripts/ and test/
build      PASS
test       PASS   67 tests, 7 files (was 0)
audit      PASS   0 high advisories (was 9)
```

---

## P0 — the launch blockers

### C-1 · One founder could overwrite another's records
Four write paths authenticated the caller and then acted on a record id the *client* supplied. `requireSelf()` answers "are you who you say you are", never "is this row yours" — and every id in this app is chosen by the client.

Reproduced first, all returning **HTTP 200** from a second founder's session:

| action | effect |
|---|---|
| `save-thread` | victim's title/state replaced, **every message deleted** |
| `save-checkin` | victim's attention score rewritten 20 → 99 |
| `save-decision` | victim's decision closed, outcome set to attacker text |
| `delete-checkin` | victim's check-in deleted outright |

The ownership check went into `src/db/index.ts`, not the API layer, so a future caller that forgets it cannot reintroduce the bug. Ordering matters in `upsertThread`: the `DELETE FROM messages` runs in the same transaction, so scoping only the `INSERT` would still have wiped the victim's messages.

`test/cross-tenant.test.ts` is the cornerstone — **4 failures before, 9/9 after**.

### C-2 · Founder prose reached organizers with no opt-in
`detectDecision` stores `text.split(" ").slice(0,9).join(" ")` — the founder's own first nine words, unaltered — and the decisions endpoint returned them verbatim to any organizer. The regex that triggers it fires on exactly the loaded messages. Verified before the fix, an organizer reading a founder who had shared nothing:

> `"Should I fire my cofounder Mikko before the Kiilto demo"`

Non-owners now get the *shape* of a decision and none of the prose. The comment claiming decisions were "already summary-level by construction" is gone; nothing summarised.

Also removed the coach card's `liveDecisions`/`liveCheckins` plumbing, which fed the **organizer's own** records into a founder's card under "Still open for them". `/api/cohort` never sent `live`, so it was inert — but only by accident.

### C-3 · Live HIGH SSRF in Astro
`astro 6.3.7` → `6.4.8`, closing GHSA-2pvr-wf23-7pc7 (Host-header SSRF), which was reachable behind Render's proxy. **19 vulnerabilities (9 high) → 5 (0 high).** The three residual Astro advisories need Astro 7 and are unreachable here — no `transition:*` directives, no `astro:transitions`, no spread props (greps in the commit).

### C-4 · No backups, with data loss now user-reachable
Daily `VACUUM INTO` snapshot → gzip → Cloudflare R2 (EU), with retention, plus `scripts/backup-db.ts` and `scripts/restore-db.ts`.

**The previously documented procedure did not work.** A database with 500 rows and the connection open has a 4 KB `.db` and a 2 MB `-wal`; copying the `.db` alone produces a file that will not open in either mode (`SQLITE_CANTOPEN` readonly, `SQLITE_MISUSE` read-write). A test asserts a raw copy never recovers the full row set.

Restore drill, run against this branch:

```
integrity_check: ok
users 2 · threads 7 · messages 21 · decisions 3 · checkins 5
```

Matching the source exactly. The timer lives in the web process because a Render cron service cannot mount the web service's disk.

---

## P1

- **H-1 · Organizer → founder takeover.** "Reset password" returned the setup link *in the response body*; any organizer could redeem it and be issued a session as that founder. Links now go to the founder's own address via Resend (EU) and are returned to nobody. It **fails closed** — unconfigured email returns 503 rather than falling back to handing over the link. Backed by a new `admin_audit` table recording every admin mutation (including failed-email attempts), and a reset email that tells the founder a reset they did not request means someone was in their account.
- **H-2 · No body size limit.** 20 MB accepted in 112 ms onto a 1 GB disk. Now 413 over 1 MB, plus per-field caps. Rejecting needed care: replying without draining the body desynchronises the keep-alive connection and the *next* request hangs — caught by the tests after a single-request curl check passed.
- **H-3 · Unthrottled paid endpoint.** 20 calls/user/minute with `Retry-After`; history trimmed to the most recent 40 turns under 60k chars.
- **H-4 · Deletion broken and silent.** Children now deleted in one transaction. The 500 had an *empty body*, so `await res.json()` rejected before reading an error — button disabled, nothing shown. Every branch returns JSON now.
- **H-5 · Reflections invented content.** `seedThemes` — three hardcoded names with zero-filled arcs — was rendered to every founder identically, never persisted, and filtered on a literal allow-list of those same three names. Themes are now derived server-side from real signals. Surfaced a real bug: `weekForDate` returns null before the sprint starts (9 Sep), so today every signal was dropped; pre-sprint dates now clamp to week 1.

## P2 / P3

Typecheck 0 errors — 10 genuine ones fixed properly, the `bun:sqlite` named-parameter noise described in `src/types/bun-sqlite.d.ts` after verifying the runtime behaviour, not suppressed with 28 ignores · uniform `ON DELETE` policy via a versioned migration (`PRAGMA user_version`), verified against a database in the old shape *and* a copy of the real local database · S-7 login timing oracle (1.5 ms vs 60 ms) closed with a decoy verify · S-8 unbounded failure map bounded · S-10 upstream errors no longer relayed (a full Cloudflare 502 page was reaching the browser) · BUG-3 silent check-in loss · atomic invite redemption · `set-thread-shared` reports the real state · blueprint drift (`SPRINT_START_DATE` was missing, so a rebuild would have pinned the cohort to week 1 forever and reported nobody needing attention) · error tracking · self-hosted fonts · CSP · non-root container · devDeps pruned · CI gate · README corrected · stale Hetzner scripts and dead `infra/` removed.

**Persona:** Paul Graham de-named to a generic archetype that says what it is if asked; **Mårten kept untouched** so Package 2 has no collision. Also deleted a dead duplicate of both system prompts from `FounderOS.tsx` — never read, shipped to every browser, and a trap for Package 2.

**Mobile:** signed in through the real setup flow and measured at 390px. No horizontal overflow; three tap targets under 40px including the send button at 36px. Raised to 44px and re-measured clean.

---

## Deliberately not done

- **Splitting `FounderOS.tsx`** (1797 → 1730). Extracting the coach views means moving the shared design tokens too — ~400 lines with zero UI test coverage, on the eve of a security merge. WP3 adds a sibling component anyway, so this does not block it.
- **Pagination** — no founder will have enough rows this cohort for it to matter.
- **Accessibility audit** — needs a real audit tool and a human; the heatmap encoding meaning in colour with only a `title` attribute is the known problem.

---

## Human follow-up (required before invites go out)

1. **Anthropic console** — set a monthly spend cap. Independent backstop for H-3.
2. **Resend** — create the account, verify the sending domain, set `RESEND_API_KEY` and `RESEND_FROM` in Render. **Adding accounts fails with 503 until this exists.**
3. **Cloudflare R2** — create an **EU-jurisdiction** bucket and API token; set `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY`, `R2_BUCKET`, `R2_ENDPOINT`.
4. **Error tracking** — provision an EU-region Sentry project, set `SENTRY_DSN` (optional; de

author: tomarra
body:
## Problem

Two user-visible strings were hardcoded English, against the convention that user-facing strings belong in `BikeBuddyKit/Localizable.strings`.

**Theme picker** — `AppearanceMode.displayName` is what the Settings → Appearance picker renders for each option:

```swift
case .automatic: return "Automatic"
case .light: return "Light"
case .dark: return "Dark"
```

The picker's own label (`SettingsThemeLabel`) and its section header (`SettingsAppearanceGroup`) are both localized, so a translated build would show a translated "Theme" label above three English options.

**About screen** — `SettingsAboutView` built its label by interpolation:

```swift
return version == build ? "Version \(version)" : "Version \(version) (\(build))"
```

## Fix

Six new keys: `SettingsThemeAutomatic` / `Light` / `Dark`, and `SettingsAboutVersionLabel` / `SettingsAboutVersionWithBuildLabel`.

The version-with-build variant uses positional specifiers (`%1$@ (%2$@)`) so a translation can reorder them.

`AppearanceMode.swift` picks up `import BikeBuddyKit` for the `.bikeBuddyKit` bundle accessor.

47 tests pass; SwiftLint `--strict` clean.

author: mattlorimor
body:
Closes #101. Eslami and Dayan, [Memento Filter](https://doi.org/10.1145/3698820) (SIGMOD 2025).

**What it is.** `Grafite` (#111) answers "is anything in [a, b]?" but is built once and never changed. Memento inserts, deletes and grows, giving up nothing on robustness — which is what makes a range filter usable behind a B-tree rather than only behind a write-once index.

Each key is cut in two: the low bits, the *memento*, are as many as the widest range you mean to ask about; everything above is the *prefix*. Prefixes partition the universe into blocks of that width, and the filter stores per occupied block a fingerprint plus the mementos of the keys inside it — the exact positions those keys hold. A range no wider than a block touches at most two, so a query is two lookups rather than a search.

## Measured

| Workload | False positive rate |
| --- | --- |
| Random empty ranges | 0.265% |
| Ranges placed immediately after each key | 0.213% |

**Those agreeing is the result.** The second workload collapses heuristic range filters; it does nothing here because a memento is a piece of the key rather than a hash of it, so aiming queries at the data buys nothing. A test pins the *comparison*, not either number.

Also: no false negatives across expansions and chains; deletes removed 20,000 of 20,000 with nothing else lost; dense blocks answer point queries with **no false positives at all** over 118,000 absent keys, the mementos being exact.

**Compact keepsake-box encoding included.** Keys sharing a block share one stored fingerprint: the same 256,000 keys cost **41.0 bits each spread one to a block and 20.5 packed sixty-four to a block**. Sparse data gets no saving, which the README says plainly.

## Why it needs its own table

Expansion moves a fingerprint's low bit into the address. Here the bits below the fingerprint are the key's own, so spending one would migrate key data into an address and answer about a key nobody stored. The memento therefore sits *below* the fluid fingerprint. The substrate change this predicted — reserving zero in the slot encoding — landed in #113 before that format shipped.

## Testing

23 tests across the filter and the codec, plus the shared suites (round-trip by answers over 30,000 keys and 20,000 ranges, empty case, read-as-another, flipped-bit corruption sweep, four hostile payloads, golden fixture pinned three ways and verified load-bearing). No span-overload entry: this filter takes numbers.

**Mutation table — 17 hand-applied, 13 killed outright. Both survivors were real holes, not equivalences:**

- **M8** (a box's keys no longer sorted) is a *false negative* waiting to happen: a box stores its smallest and largest up front to exclude ranges, so an unordered box excludes queries whose answer it holds. It survived because every test I'd written added keys ascending, so appending kept boxes ordered whether the code sorted them or not. Then it survived *again* after I added a back-to-front test — because the sorting existed in **two places**, filter and table, and mutating one left the other. Same duplication the InfiniFilter table found, caught the same way. Deduplicated; now dies to two tests.
- **M1** (slot count not reduced on rewrite) is invisible to correctness: nothing answers wrongly, the table just doubles on its own schedule and costs twice the memory. Pinned by the dense-versus-sparse space comparison, which does double duty.

I also wrote that space assertion before measuring it and it failed by 16 bytes — the spare word each table carries. Measured, then pinned with the slack explained.

## Verification

- Clean `dotnet build -c Release -warnaserror`: exit 0, zero warnings (exit code read unpiped).
- `dotnet test -c Release`: 688/688, up from 658.
- README anchors machine-checked; the code sample compiles and runs as printed.

body:
## The claim

**`qn.6q` declined a WebSocket event for config changes on a premise that was never true. The decision stands; the reason is replaced with the measurement.**

Found by the Operator testing `qn.6q` on staging: a hand-edit **applied server-side** and the open Settings page kept showing the old value until reloaded by hand.

## What the spec said, and why it was wrong

`docs/specs/qn.6q/qn.6q.md:193`:

> *a reload has no better claim, and the Settings page already re-reads on focus.*

It does not:

| mechanism | state |
|---|---|
| `refetchOnWindowFocus` | **`false`** — `ui/src/lib/queryClient.ts:9`, app-wide |
| `refetchInterval` on the config query | **absent** — `useConfig` sets `queryKey` and `queryFn` and nothing else |
| a config-change event | **declined** twice |

`staleTime: 5_000` means it refreshes on remount, so navigating away and back is current. **Staying on the page never updates** — which is exactly what testing a hand-edit looks like.

## The decision is unchanged

Declining the event is still right, and `qn.6g` rung-ruled decision 4 declined it for the write path on reasoning this rung does not improve on. What changes is that the bullet no longer rests on a mechanism that does not exist.

**The behaviour is filed as quince#1162 rather than fixed here**, because it is user-visible and the options differ in cost — a `refetchInterval` on one query, a per-query focus refetch, an event, or nothing plus honest copy on a screen whose subtitle invites hand-editing. That is a ruling, not a rung-local call.

**It matters more since this rung than before it.** A hand-edit used to do nothing until a restart, so a stale page *agreed* with reality. Now the page and the daemon genuinely disagree.

## Why this is its own PR

I first committed it onto quince#1161's branch, which carries a different claim (`sessions.allow_insecure_transport` is live). Two claims, one PR — the thing I have been holding this rung to all day. Split back out; quince#1161 is one commit again.

`make privacy-check REF=origin/main...HEAD` — exit **0**. Docs-only, one bullet.

`deploy: not applicable — no runnable change`

Refs quince#1094, quince#1162

author: jegr78
body:
Part of the roster synchronisation work for #74. **Fourth of five stacked pull requests**, targeting the third. Merge in order.

This is the one to read carefully: it is the only pull request in the stack that writes to the roster.

## What this adds

The preview is the contract. What a board approved is what runs — nothing is re-resolved and nothing is re-read from the file, so a roster that moved between the review and the click cannot be written over by a change set that no longer describes it. If anybody the preview would touch has changed since it was taken, the run is refused and nothing is written. Only the people it would touch count, so an unrelated correction elsewhere does not block a club's import.

The whole run is one transaction. A change set whose last row fails leaves nothing behind: not a person, not a membership, not a reference. Proven by deactivating a membership type between the preview and the run and counting rows across all four tables afterwards.

## The two ways this could hurt an instance

**It cannot lock a club out.** A membership ending withdraws `MEMBER` from the account. An account holding another role keeps it and stays enabled, so one holding `ADMIN` always does. An account whose only role was `MEMBER` is disabled and its sessions end. **No snapshot ever enables an account** — a board disabled it for a reason no membership system knows, and a file listing that person as current is not evidence against it. That guarantee holds today only because no code path calls `enable()`, which is exactly the kind of thing that disappears when somebody later adds a reasonable-looking line, so it has its own test.

**It cannot loosen anybody's rules.** `dataexchange` never touches `person`, `user_account` or `member`. Everything goes through `RosterSyncService` in `member`, which goes through `RosterService`, so the roster's guards keep their single door. The property is asserted as a **booking**, not as a role set: an officer whose membership the snapshot ended is refused by a card requiring `MEMBER`, and the same booking succeeds before the snapshot, so the test cannot pass vacuously. The card in it declares `allowedRoles` explicitly, because the seeded member card has none and permits everyone.

## Concurrency, and why no deadlock path exists

Executions of one source serialise on `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. The lock uses the **two-int form** keyed by a namespace and the source id, so it cannot collide with `AdministratorLock` or `BootstrapLock` at all — those use the single-bigint form, which PostgreSQL keeps in a separate lock space — and two different sources never block each other.

No deadlock path exists between them: an import never acquires `AdministratorLock`, because it never routes through the role-change operation that takes it, and person rows are locked in id order so two imports touching the same people queue instead of crossing. `ConcurrentExecutionTest` drives two real transactions on two threads.

A successful run supersedes every preview of that source **including its own**, so re-executing a reviewed snapshot is impossible rather than merely unwise. It forgets the preview's change set on the way out. The run log keeps the hash and the counts and never a copy of the roster — §11's data minimisation is not satisfied by a second roster in an import table.

Both single comparisons the plan flagged were mutation-tested: an always-fresh staleness check and an always-below threshold each kill a test.

## Two corrections to the schema, edited in place

Running this end to end surfaced two gaps that the earlier pull requests could not see:

1. **A person in this product cannot exist without an email address**, so a source that cannot supply one could never create anybody. `EMAIL` is now a required column of a source's mapping. Requiring the column is not requiring every cell: a row whose address is empty fails on its own and the rest of the file resolves.
2. **A created member holds a membership type**, and a club may not export a category at all. A source now names the type its new records take; a mapped category still wins where the file carries one.

Both are corrections to what `V22` should have said and are **edited into it**. Nothing is released, and a repair migration for a table added on an unmerged branch would be a fossil of this session rather than a design. This is why the stack must merge in order.

## From the whole-stack self-review

Three defects were found by reviewing the finished stack and are fixed in this pull request. Each was reproduced with a probe before being believed.

**A cell this product cannot store reached the roster as a change.** An empty name, a value with a line break, one longer than the column allows, or something that is not an email address passed the preview as a clean change and then hit `RosterService`'s own guard during execution — an `IllegalStateException`, which is a 500 and the honest answer only when a caller skipped validation that runs somewhere else. Here nothing ran it: the import is a second write path to `person` and never had the constraints `PersonRequest` enforces at the web edge. Such a row is now a row error in the preview, and `PersonFieldLimits` is the one place both paths read the rules from. The security pass raised the same gap from the other side.

**The staleness check could not see a creation.** It compares fingerprints of people the change set names, and a creation names nobody yet. A member number linked between the preview and the run therefore produced a second record for somebody the roster already held, and the unique constraint answered with a raw integrity violation instead of the typed refusal this endpoint documents.

**Deleting a source checked references and not runs.** A source that had run and whose references were later unlinked could not be deleted at all — a foreign key violation on `import_run` instead of an answer. It is now refused deliberately, and for good: the run log is history, the same argument that put the `409` there for references.

Two smaller ones from the same pass: the preview is read *after* the source lock rather than before it, so the superseded check no longer leans on the unique constraint on `import_run` to catch what it missed; and the affected person ids are computed once instead of twice.

`ValidationMessageCoverageTest` only knew `CsvSnapshot.RowError`, so a code passed to `ResolvedChangeSet.RowError` would have shipped without a message in either bundle. Its pattern now covers both — verified by pointing the new code at a key no bundle defines and watching the guard fail.

## Verification

`./mvnw clean verify` green.

author: mrjvnsmth
body:
## Summary
Extends self-improvement-loop.md with the counterweight to its own governing principle. The retro loop is reactive by construction: misses and failures are its inputs, so it never learns what nobody has looked at, and attention follows noise while quiet subsystems stay quiet. Documents the fix as run in the production system these essays describe: a coverage ledger (one row per domain, never-explored outranks any dated row), strict stalest-first rotation instead of hand-picked favorites, targetless read-only exploration that hunts absent facts (no instrument, no read path, no docs) as hard as wrong ones, origin-tagged findings so the looking-versus-breaking balance becomes a monthly count, and checked-clean recorded as a real result.

Names the deliberate contradiction rather than hiding it: this rotation IS scheduled, because unexplored territory generates no evidence to trigger on, so waiting for a trigger waits forever. The mitigation is stated (slow schedule, cheap passes, and a rotation that re-explores fresh domains has turned back into churn). Sizing section says to add it last, and only once the estate outgrows what one person holds in their head. docs/README.md index row updated.

## Test plan
Zero em-dashes; provenance-leak guard clean on the diff.

## What's NOT in scope
No coverage-ledger template or runner; the pattern is a table plus a rotation rule, and the essay's existing convention is to describe fleet machinery rather than ship it.

body:
Part of the roster synchronisation work for #74. **Last of five stacked pull requests**, targeting the fourth. Merge in order.

## What this adds

A preview holds a club's whole membership list in the change set resolved from it, and none of it is needed once the window for executing it has passed. A scheduled sweep drops it and keeps the row, its hash and its counts, which is what an audit of what was reviewed needs and is not personal data.

A swept preview is refused rather than executed. That path already existed for an expired one; the sweep makes it reachable, and the test asserts the roster is untouched afterwards rather than only that an exception was thrown.

## Why the sweep takes its cutoff as a parameter

The scheduled entry point passes the clock; the sweep itself takes an `Instant`. The alternative — a method reading the clock and a test that moves time — cannot work against a fixed test clock without either sleeping or mutating an entity through a setter that exists for no other reason. Passing the cutoff keeps the test deterministic, and the scheduled delegation has its own test.

## Operations

`COURTSIDE_IMPORT_PREVIEW_RETENTION` (7d) and `COURTSIDE_IMPORT_SWEEP_INTERVAL` (1h) are defaulted in `application.yaml` and documented in `deploy/README.md` with every other environment setting.

## What the whole stack leaves for later

- The **browser journey** for import — the API is complete, there is no admin UI yet (#81 covers the roster's browser surface).
- **Accounts from a snapshot**: a synchronisation creates people and memberships, never accounts. Bulk activation is its own piece of work.
- **Export**, which is the other half of §8.

author: robertoaraneda
body:
The last place `CONFORMANCE.md` said nothing. A reader could reasonably have assumed either that `Long` was implemented or that `Integer` was 32 bits. Neither is true.

## The divergence

The specification gives `Integer` the range −2³¹ to 2³¹−1 and adds a `Long` for −2⁶³ to 2⁶³−1, with literals of its own (`45L`) and `toLong`/`convertsToLong` to reach it. All of that is marked **Standard for Trial Use**.

This engine holds an `Integer` in Go's `int64`, so it already spans the range `Long` exists to provide:

```
3000000000                        // 3000000000
3000000000.type().name            // Integer
3000000000 is Integer             // true
2147483647 + 1                    // 2147483648
'3000000000'.convertsToInteger()  // true
```

A conforming engine answers `{ }` to the first and `false` to the last. Narrowing to 32 bits would break callers passing values FHIR itself defines a type for — R5 has `integer64`, and I checked that `Extension.valueInteger64` resolves to it in the R5 model rather than assuming it. So the range stays, documented, and `toLong`/`convertsToLong` are left out: against a 64-bit `Integer` they are `toInteger` and `convertsToInteger` under another name.

## A gap found while writing it, recorded as a gap

Arithmetic wraps at the end of the range:

```
9223372036854775807 + 1     // -9223372036854775808
```

Go's `int64` overflow reaching the surface. A literal too large for an `int64` is read as a `Decimal` — `9223372036854775808` answers with itself — but a sum that crosses the boundary gets no such treatment.

Whether it should signal an error or return empty is not settled by the specification for `Integer` either, so it is written down as an open question rather than fixed by widening the type. It is not presented as a decision, because it isn't one.

## Verification

Every example in the section was executed against the engine, including the model lookup behind the `integer64` claim. No code changes; conformance and lint unaffected.

With this, every known failure and every unimplemented function in the file has a recorded reason: `pathname`, `htmlChecks`, `%terminologies`, `Long`, and the eight R4 / fourteen R5 suite cases.

author: lucasschirm
body:
## Summary

Phase 3 of the Claude Code Session Data Sync plan: SHA-256 hashing of sanitized content and the delta engine that powers incremental uploads.

- `sha256Hex()`: SHA-256 of sanitized content (not original) using `node:crypto`
- `buildS3ObjectKey()`: deterministic key `<projectId>/<sessionId>/<scope>/<relativePath>`
- `selectSanitizer()`: maps artifact paths to existing sanitizers; session `*.jsonl` transcripts left raw
- `processDelta()`: the delta engine — sanitize → hash → compare against `lastUploadedHash` → skip unchanged / upload changed → advance state only on confirmed success
- `getTriggerScope()`: maps all 9 triggers to 4 scopes (bulk, watcher-delta, hash-filtered, session-end-final)
- `buildSessionManifest()`: records SHA-256 per artifact, uploaded as `runtime/manifest.json` on session-end
- Per-trigger metrics: `filesDiscovered`, `filesChanged`, `filesUnchanged`, `filesUploaded`, `bytesDiscovered`, `bytesChanged`
- Failed uploads: `recordArtifactFailure()` leaves `lastUploadedHash` un-advanced; next trigger re-detects as changed
- 21 unit tests

author: abidlabs
body:
### `31829ac4b` — detect when someone deliberately leaves the page

Browsers do not expose "the user closed this tab", so the queue currently cannot tell an abandoned tab apart from one the person switched away from. This commit adds that signal to the client, and nothing else: `on_deliberate_exit()` replaces the `beforeunload` listener in both app shells with `pagehide`, gated on two conditions — the page is not being parked in the back/forward cache (`event.persisted`), and it is still visible when the event arrives. The second condition is the useful one: the spec fires `pagehide` *before* the visibility state flips to hidden, so a page that still reads `visible` is being destroyed by a foreground action, whereas a page that already reads `hidden` was backgrounded earlier and is now being reclaimed by the browser or the OS. `beforeunload` cannot draw that line and is unreliable on mobile, where it frequently never fires.

| what the person did | events fired | reported as deliberate? |
|---|---|---|
| closed the foreground tab, reloaded, or navigated away | `pagehide`, `persisted=false`, still `visible` | **yes** |
| switched to another tab or window on desktop | `visibilitychange` only — no `pagehide` | no |
| switched apps, opened another tab, or locked the screen on mobile | `visibilitychange`, `freeze`, often `pagehide` with `persisted=true` | no |
| left the tab open and the OS reclaimed it under memory pressure | `pagehide`, `persisted=false`, already `hidden` | no |
| lost network for a few seconds | nothing — the page is alive | no |
| closed a tab that was not in the foreground (⌘W on an inactive tab, iOS tab switcher) | `pagehide`, `persisted=false`, already `hidden` | no — accepted miss |
| crashed, force quit, ran out of memory or battery | nothing | no — accepted miss |

The rule is deliberately one-sided. Reading "deliberate" into someone merely switching tabs would discard work they expect to find waiting, while reading "not deliberate" into a real exit only delays cleanup, so every ambiguous case resolves to not deliberate. The last two rows are the price of that choice and are documented on the helper: a background close is indistinguishable from a system reclaim, and a crash fires nothing at all. Any consumer therefore has to treat this as an optimisation for the common case on top of a server-side timeout, never as a signal it can depend on.

No behavior change on its own — `on_deliberate_exit(() => app.close())` does what the old listener did, just in fewer situations. Five assertions cover the matrix against real Chromium, plus one for the server-rendered case where there is no DOM to listen to.

---

### `2b555dbd9` — stop an event on a deadline instead of the moment its client vanishes

Losing a connection was read as proof that somebody left: the SSE handler called `clean_events` and the work was gone. But every row of the table above that involves a dropped socket looks identical from the server, so that reading was wrong for the two cases that matter most. Events now carry `cancel_at`, and the three things that can end an event set it rather than acting immediately.

| what happens | before | now |
|---|---|---|
| mobile backgrounds the tab, or the network drops for a few seconds | the event is removed at once | `cancel_at` = one hour out (`GRADIO_QUEUE_DISCONNECT_TTL`); the work keeps running |
| a stream attaches for the session | nothing to attach to | `cancel_at` cleared — the session is reprieved |
| a stale stream's disconnect is noticed after a reconnect | — | ignored; the connection that dropped no longer owns the session |
| the client reports a deliberate exit (`POST /queue/close`) | nothing — the server waited to notice the socket, up to 10s | `cancel_at` = now |
| `POST /cancel` | cancelled the task, closed the iterator, told the client | unchanged, via the shared path |
| the heartbeat connection drops with work in flight | ran `unload` immediately, underneath the running job | deferred until the work stops |
| the heartbeat drops with nothing in flight | ran `unload` | unchanged |

Stopping an event was three partial implementations that each did a different subset of the work — which is why closing a tab did not stop a job the way pressing stop did:

| | `/cancel` | SSE disconnect | heartbeat disconnect |
|---|---|---|---|
| cancel the awaiting asyncio task | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| remove it if still queued | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| mark `alive = False` | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ |
| close the iterator | ✅ | only later, in `process_events` | ❌ |
| release a streaming event waiting for input | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |
| tell the client | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| run `unload` | ❌ | ❌ | ✅ |

All three now go through `Queue.cancel_events`, which does the whole set, with `notify` separating "somebody is waiting to be released" from "nobody is listening". `clean_events` had no callers left and is deleted; iterator teardown becomes `App.close_iterator`, since the app owns `iterators` and `iterators_to_reset`. `unload` likewise had to exist in two places once the queue needed it, so it is now a single `routes.close_session` called by both the heartbeat and the queue. Cancelled events are not waited on before that runs: a blocking call cannot be interrupted, so holding the handlers until it returns on its own would only delay cleanup that used to happen at once.

Two things this deliberately does **not** do yet. The reprieve works, but nothing reaches it outside the tests — a reloaded page gets a fresh `session_hash` and the client does not reopen a broken stream, so both are still one-way trips. And a job that finishes while nobody is listening still loses its output, so "your work survived" does not yet mean "you will see it". A deliberate exit therefore stops the work immediately rather than after a grace period; the grace only becomes meaningful once a reloading page can reattach, since a reload is indistinguishable from a close at the moment the client reports it.

Tests: seven cases in `test_queueing.py` covering a dropped stream keeping its event, the reprieve, a replaced stream being unable to condemn the new one, a deliberate exit stopping the work and running `unload`, and `/cancel` still completing a queued event; `/queue/close` auth in `test_routes.py`; two client tests for the `keepalive` beacon, including that it carries `Authorization` and fires only once. Also green: `test_blocks.py`, `test_routes.py`, `test_server.py`, `test_chat_interface.py`, the JS client suite in both browser and node modes, and the full JS unit suite.

---

### `78d609055` — keep a job's output so a reloaded page can collect it by job id

Surviving the loss of a client is only half the promise: the output produced while nobody was listening still went nowhere, because delivery goes through `pending_messages_per_session` — a single queue per session whose `get()` *removes* the message, so it cannot be read by anyone but that session's own stream. Events now keep what they send, and one can be followed on its own through `GET /queue/event/{event_id}`, which replays what the event has already sent and then streams the rest.

**Reattaching by job id rather than by session hash is the point.** The job keeps running under the session it was submitted from, because its `gr.State` is bound there; a reloaded page gets a fresh session hash and therefore the cleared state it is entitled to. Only the output crosses over. Reclaiming the old session instead — the obvious shortcut — would carry that state into a page that has otherwise started from scratch, silently and only when a job happened to be running at the moment of the reload. The job id is also server-issued and unguessable (`uuid4`), unlike the client-chosen `session_hash` (`Math.random()`), so it is the better capability token as well.

| | `session_hash` | `event_id` |
|---|---|---|
| issued by | the client, `Math.random()` | the server, `uuid4` |
| identifies | identity, delivery **and** `gr.State` | one job |
| reattaching implies

body:
Salvages the parts of #21 that were still worth having, rebased onto current main.

`format = "setuptools"` and `checkInputs` are both deprecated in nixpkgs. Four packages still used them:

- `pretty-midi`, `mirdata`: `format = "setuptools"` → `pyproject = true` with `setuptools` in `build-system`

`CLAUDE.md` gets the documentation half of #21, corrected where that PR overstated things (`format` is deprecated and warns, it does not error) and trimmed to conventions this repo actually follows.

## What I left out of #21

That PR also rewrote all 52 packages from `rec` to the `finalAttrs` pattern, dropped `wheel` from every `build-system`, and added `pytestCheckHook` to packages that were not running tests before. Five months on it conflicts across 54 files, and turning tests on for packages that have never run them is the kind of change that wants to land one package at a time so CI can attribute each failure. The `finalAttrs` conversion is pure churn here since nothing overrides these derivations. I would rather do that as its own sweep than smuggle it in behind a docs change, so #21 is closed in favour of this.

## Testing

Local verification was not possible in this environment — the sandbox network policy blocks fetching nixpkgs, so `nix flake check` cannot evaluate. Relying on CI to build the three changed packages.

author: andreabade
body:
## What

The Ultralytics classification defaults (crop area 0.5–1.0, RandAugment, random erasing, HSV jitter) gave `YOLO26N_CLS` a materially stronger augmentation regime than the twenty `torchvision`/`timm` models, which share the transforms in `configs/augmentations.yaml`.

Matching it as closely as the API allows moves the model from **0.9856 to 0.9340** test accuracy — from 1st to 19th of 22. Epoch budget, input resolution and learning-rate endpoints were already matched, so the gap is the augmentation.

## Why it matters

The previous leaderboard result was a training-recipe artefact, not an architectural one. Consequences already propagated to the manuscript:

- Leader is now `Ensemble_CNN` (0.9684, **unchanged** — no other model was retrained)
- Size↔accuracy Spearman collapses from −0.50 (p = 0.020) to −0.26 (p = 0.26), no longer significant
- McNemar: 106/231 significant after FDR (was 115); the ensemble does *not* differ significantly from DenseNet201, MobileNetV3-Large, ResNet152 or NFNet
- Error-free selective-classification coverage: 86% → 66.7%

## Also in this PR

`src/scale_robustness.py` hard-coded `YOLO26N_CLS` as both the model name and the load path, so it could not follow the leader once that changed. It now takes `--model`, defaults to the top of `ranking_models.csv`, handles `torchvision`/`timm` alongside `ultralytics`, and averages members for the ensemble. Scales are swept in a single pass over the loader because building it fills the RAM cache.

## Note

Aggregates, figures, manuscript and built PDF/DOCX are already updated in the working tree; those paths are gitignored, so this PR carries the `src/` changes only.

author: lucasschirm
body:
## Summary

Phase 3 of the Claude Code Session Data Sync plan: a harness-agnostic `StorageAdapter` interface and an S3 implementation using the official AWS SDK, with bounded retry and credential-safe error handling.

- `StorageAdapter` interface: `putObject` (required), `getObject`/`headObject` (optional) — independent of S3
- `S3StorageAdapter`: uses `@aws-sdk/client-s3` (`S3Client`, `PutObjectCommand`); no manual S3 signing
- `buildObjectKey()`: deterministic layout `<projectId>/<sessionId>/{manifest.json, session/, workspace/, global/, runtime/}`; percent-encodes segments; rejects absolute paths, `..` traversal, unsupported scopes, over-long keys
- Idempotent PUTs: same artifact → same key + SHA256; S3 overwrites duplicates harmlessly; `sha256` metadata header for content-addressed verification
- `withRetry()`: bounded exponential backoff; retryable (5xx, 408, 429, network timeout, connection reset, rate limiting) vs non-retryable (invalid credentials, invalid bucket, permission denied, malformed config, invalid object key)
- Credential safety: `mapS3Error` builds messages from error catalog descriptions + HTTP status only; raw AWS exception strings never in `message`/`toString()`; credentials only passed to SDK client constructor, never logged/persisted
- Cross-invocation retry: implicit via delta engine, not a separate queue in storage
- 47 unit tests: adapter contract, key normalization, retry classification, idempotent PUT (incl. concurrent duplicate), credential-safe errors, S3 command mapping (mocked SDK)

No real S3 calls in unit tests (mock-based). Full S3 integration suite owned by TSK0016. No edits to top-level barrel or `package.json` (AWS SDK pre-added).
